LiteLLM auth bypass: malformed Host header on admin/management routes (CVE-2026-49468) AIExploitation High
Hunts the root cause of CVE-2026-49468 — a crafted Host header used to make get_request_route() evaluate a different route than FastAPI dispatched. A legitimate Host is only hostname[:port]; any Host carrying a slash, '@', whitespace or '..' reaching a LiteLLM management endpoint (/key,/user,/team,...) is the injection signature. Rationale: Uses the article's exact root-cause (Host-header-driven route evaluation in get_request_route) and the confirmed LiteLLM management route prefixes (/key,/user,/team,...). A Host value containing path/@/whitespace chars is never legitimate, making this high-fidelity. defender_kql/falcon/cloudwatch/datadog empty: Defender XDR, Falcon FDR and the listed Datadog/CloudTrail sources do not ingest reverse-proxy HTTP access logs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4xpc-pv4p-pm3w • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/litellm/CVE-2026-49468/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/litellm-vulnerability-host-header-injection/ • https://deepwiki.com/BerriAI/litellm/3.5-management-endpoints-and-multi-tenancy
ATT&CKT1190 T1036
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanners (Burp, OWASP ZAP, Nuclei, Nessus) deliberately fuzzing the Host header during an authorised pentest
  • A misconfigured upstream proxy that forwards a comma-joined X-Forwarded-Host chain into the Host field
  • Service-mesh / sidecar that rewrites Host to include a path-style virtual-host
  • IPv6 literal Host values bracketed oddly by a buggy client (rare)
Suppression filter
| where not (HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has_any ("Nessus","Nuclei","ZAP","sqlmap","masscan") and SrcIpAddr in ("10.0.0.0/8"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests from the source IP/Host pair; confirm the Host value is malformed (contains /,@,space,..) and which management endpoint it targeted, and whether the response was 2xx (successful bypass) vs 401/403. 2) Contain: if any 2xx returned, treat as compromise — rotate the LiteLLM master key and all virtual keys, and block the source IP at the upstream WAF/LB; confirm proxy is upgraded to >=1.84.0. 3) Hunt: review /key, /user, /team write operations from that source for created keys or deleted users; correlate with UC for unauthenticated admin writes and rapid state-change abuse.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any ("/key/","/user/","/team/","/model/","/customer/","/spend/","/organization/")
| where isnotempty(HttpHostName)
| where HttpHostName matches regex @"[\\/@\s]" or HttpHostName contains ".."
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, UserAgent=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstHostname, DstPortNumber
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LiteLLM unauthenticated successful write to management endpoint (CVE-2026-49468) AIExploitation High
Hard exploit signal for CVE-2026-49468: a state-changing request (POST/PUT/DELETE) to a LiteLLM management route (/key,/user,/team,/model,/spend,...) that returns 2xx with NO Authorization / API-key header present. These routes must never accept unauthenticated writes; a success here means the Host-header auth gate was bypassed. Rationale: Combines the article's management-route list with the invariant that these routes require an API key — a 2xx write with an empty Authorization header is the bypass success condition. Splunk CIM Web has no Authorization-header field so its SPL surfaces unauth-write candidates by method+route+2xx only (auth-header check noted as Sentinel-only); Sigma skipped because the discriminating field (absent auth header) is not in the neutral webserver schema. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch/Datadog empty — no HTTP access-log ingestion there. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4xpc-pv4p-pm3w • https://deepwiki.com/BerriAI/litellm/3.5-management-endpoints-and-multi-tenancy • https://gbhackers.com/critical-litellm-flaw/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • LiteLLM configured with master-key-in-cookie or session auth so the Authorization header is legitimately absent on UI-driven writes
  • Internal automation that authenticates via a custom header your log pipeline doesn't map to HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization
  • Log pipeline strips/redacts the Authorization header before indexing, making every authed request look unauthenticated
  • Health/readiness tooling that POSTs to a benign management route
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the write actually mutated state (response body / subsequent /key/list) and that no auth header or session cookie was present; verify the proxy version is <1.84.0. 2) Contain: rotate the LiteLLM master key and revoke any virtual keys created in the window; block the source IP upstream and force-upgrade to >=1.84.0 or place behind a Host-validating WAF. 3) Hunt: enumerate every object created/modified/deleted by that source across /key,/user,/team,/spend; pivot to the malformed-Host UC to confirm the injection vector and to the rapid-state-change UC for follow-on abuse.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod in~ ("POST","PUT","DELETE")
| where Url has_any ("/key/","/user/","/team/","/model/","/customer/","/spend/","/organization/")
| where HttpStatusCode in ("200","201","202","204")
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, UserAgent=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LiteLLM auth bypass: 401-then-200 to same admin route with identical Host header AIExploitation High
Correlates a 401 followed by a 200/2xx on the SAME LiteLLM management endpoint from the SAME source IP carrying the SAME Host header value within 5 minutes. Persistence of the crafted Host value across the failed-then-successful pair proves the success was Host-header-driven (CVE-2026-49468), not a legitimate re-authentication. Rationale: Directly implements reviewer hypothesis #1: tying the 401 and the subsequent 2xx by identical SrcIpAddr + HttpHostName + route proves the same crafted Host value drove the bypass. Temporal/cross-row correlation so no Sigma. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch/Datadog empty — telemetry is reverse-proxy HTTP logs only. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4xpc-pv4p-pm3w • https://cybersecuritynews.com/litellm-vulnerability-host-header-injection/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user whose API key genuinely expired, refreshed it, and retried within 5 minutes from a stable Host (legitimate re-auth)
  • Automation with a retry loop that supplies the correct key on the second attempt after a transient 401
  • Shared-NAT egress where two distinct clients reuse the same source IP and Host
  • Load-balancer health re-checks producing 401 then 200 as backends recover
Suppression filter
| where HttpHostName matches regex @"[\\/@\s]" or HttpHostName contains ".."
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the Host header value on both the 401 and the 200 — if it is malformed or differs from your canonical proxy hostname, this is the bypass; if it's the normal hostname, likely benign re-auth. 2) Contain: on confirmation, block the source IP, rotate the master key and any keys minted after the 200, and verify upgrade to >=1.84.0. 3) Hunt: expand the window to capture all subsequent admin actions from the source; cross-reference the unauthenticated-write and rapid-state-change UCs.
let admin = dynamic(["/key/","/user/","/team/","/model/","/customer/","/spend/","/organization/"]);
let fails = ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where Url has_any (admin)
  | where HttpStatusCode == "401"
  | project FailTime=TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, Url;
let oks = ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where Url has_any (admin)
  | where HttpStatusCode in ("200","201","202","204")
  | project OkTime=TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, Url;
fails
| join kind=inner oks on SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName
| where OkTime between (FailTime .. FailTime + 5m)
| where Url == Url1
| project FailTime, OkTime, DelaySec=datetime_diff('second',OkTime,FailTime), SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, Url
| order by OkTime desc

LiteLLM recon probes (/health,/version,/docs) followed by admin-route access from same source AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects scripted exploitation of CVE-2026-49468: a source that fingerprints the proxy via /health, /version, /docs or /openapi.json and then pivots to management routes (/key,/user,/team,...) within 10 minutes. Probe-then-enumerate clustering from one source is the signature of an automated LiteLLM attack tool. Rationale: Implements reviewer hypothesis #4 using LiteLLM's real unauthenticated info routes (/health,/version,/docs,/openapi.json — present on the FastAPI proxy) and the confirmed management routes, bounded by a 10-minute window. Multi-event temporal correlation so no Sigma. Empty non-web platform fields for the same access-log reason. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4xpc-pv4p-pm3w • https://deepwiki.com/BerriAI/litellm/3.5-management-endpoints-and-multi-tenancy
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1046 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Kubernetes liveness/readiness probes hitting /health then a monitoring job querying management routes from the same in-cluster IP
  • API gateway / uptime monitor that crawls /docs and /openapi.json for schema diffing
  • An internal developer exploring the Swagger UI then legitimately calling /key/list with a valid key
  • CI pipeline that health-checks then provisions keys during deploy
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !startswith "10." and SrcIpAddr !startswith "172.16." and SrcIpAddr !startswith "192.168."
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP is external/unexpected and that the admin-route calls lacked valid auth or returned 2xx; whitelist known monitors/CI ranges first. 2) Contain: if admin access succeeded, block the IP, rotate keys, and patch to >=1.84.0. 3) Hunt: review the full request sequence for malformed Host headers (injection vector) and for any write operations; escalate to the unauthenticated-write and rapid-state-change UCs.

  | where Url has_any ("/health","/version","/docs","/openapi.json")
  | project ReconTime=TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr;
let admin = ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where Url has_any ("/key/","/user/","/team/","/model/","/customer/","/spend/","/organization/")
  | project AdminTime=TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode;
recon
| join kind=inner admin on SrcIpAddr
| where AdminTime between (ReconTime .. ReconTime + 10m)
| summarize ReconHits=count(), FirstRecon=min(ReconTime), FirstAdmin=min(AdminTime), AdminEndpoints=make_set(Url,20) by SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName
| order by FirstAdmin desc

LiteLLM post-bypass rapid state-changing admin writes (key/user/team mutation burst) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects post-exploitation abuse after a CVE-2026-49468 bypass: a single source issuing 5+ successful state-changing writes (key generate/delete, user new/delete, team new/delete, spend/model changes) to LiteLLM management routes within a 5-minute window. This is the scripted credential-minting / account-removal stage once auth is defeated. Rationale: Implements reviewer hypothesis #5 with LiteLLM's concrete state-changing routes (/key/generate,/key/delete,/user/new,/user/delete,/team/new,...) and a 5-in-5min burst threshold for scripted abuse; mapped to T1098 (key minting), T1531 (user/key deletion), T1565 (spend/config tampering). Threshold + windowed aggregation so no Sigma. Non-web platform fields empty — access-log-only telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4xpc-pv4p-pm3w • https://deepwiki.com/BerriAI/litellm/3.5-management-endpoints-and-multi-tenancy • https://www.danilchenko.dev/posts/litellm-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1098 T1531 T1565
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Bulk onboarding/offboarding automation that legitimately creates or deletes many keys/users/teams in a tight window
  • Terraform / IaC reconciliation run that mass-updates spend limits and models
  • A migration script re-provisioning virtual keys after a master-key rotation
  • Load test or QA suite exercising the management API
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in (dynamic(["10.0.0.0"])) and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has_any ("terraform","litellm-provisioner")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the burst source carried valid auth and is an approved automation host; pull the exact objects created/deleted (new key IDs, removed users). 2) Contain: revoke all keys generated in the window, restore deleted users/teams from backup, rotate the master key, and block the source IP; verify proxy is >=1.84.0. 3) Hunt: trace the new keys' subsequent LLM usage/egress for data exfil or cost abuse, and back-correlate to the malformed-Host and unauth-write UCs to confirm the initial bypass.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod in~ ("POST","PUT","DELETE")
| where Url has_any ("/key/generate","/key/delete","/key/update","/user/new","/user/delete","/user/update","/team/new","/team/delete","/team/update","/spend/","/model/new","/model/delete")
| where HttpStatusCode in ("200","201","202","204")
| summarize WriteCount=count(), Endpoints=make_set(Url,30), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where WriteCount >= 5
| order by LastSeen desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Node dropper fetches second stage from Hostwinds raw IP 23.254.164.92:8000
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — A Forgotten Contributor Account Compromised the Entire Mastra npm Package Scope
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] npm install pulls malicious easy-day-js dropper (setup.cjs + .pkg marker files) · [LLM] easy-day-js stealer persistence masquerading as Node tooling (NodePackages / LaunchAgent / systemd) · [LLM] Mastra easy-day-js second-stage stealer payload by SHA256 · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Cross-platform stealer RAT C2 beacon to 23.254.164.123 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
npm install pulls malicious easy-day-js dropper (setup.cjs + .pkg marker files) AIInstallation High
Hunts a build/dev host resolving the trojanized easy-day-js dependency: the package landing under node_modules\easy-day-js, its setup.cjs postinstall dropper, and the ~/.pkg_history / ~/.pkg_logs marker files the dropper writes to track installs. Article-specific because these exact filenames and the easy-day-js package path are the carrier injected into the @mastra scope. Rationale: Anchors on the exact carrier filenames named by Snyk and corroborated by Microsoft/StepSecurity: the easy-day-js node_modules path, setup.cjs postinstall dropper, and the .pkg_history/.pkg_logs markers — none of which exist on a clean host. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised-using-easy-day-js • https://socket.dev/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher detonating the sample in a sandbox/analysis VM
  • Defenders deliberately caching the malicious tarball for IR/forensics
  • A renamed-but-unrelated package legitimately named easy-day-js in an internal registry mirror (rare)
  • Backup/EDR agents re-scanning an already-quarantined node_modules tree
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host resolved easy-day-js@1.11.21/1.11.22 — check the project lockfile and whether npm install ran on/after 2026-06-17; pull the SHA256 of any setup.cjs found. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill any node-spawned detached process, and treat it as credential+wallet exposure — force-reset npm tokens, cloud creds, and browser-stored secrets used on that host; revoke/rotate any wallet seed phrases. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same DeviceId for outbound connections to 23.254.164.92/.123 and persistence under C:\ProgramData\NodePackages; sweep CI runners and other dev laptops sharing the lockfile.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("setup.cjs",".pkg_history",".pkg_logs")) or FolderPath has @"\node_modules\easy-day-js\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("setup.cjs",".pkg_history",".pkg_logs") or TargetFilePath has @"\node_modules\easy-day-js\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Malicious easy-day-js npm Dropper Artifacts (Mastra Supply Chain)

Node dropper fetches second stage from Hostwinds raw IP 23.254.164.92:8000 AIDelivery High
Hunts the easy-day-js dropper's second-stage download: an outbound connection to the hardcoded Hostwinds host 23.254.164.92 on port 8000 (https://23.254.164.92:8000/update/49890878), typically initiated by node.exe after TLS verification is disabled. High-fidelity because the IP+port are dedicated attacker infrastructure confirmed by multiple vendors. Rationale: Uses the verbatim dropper URL host/port (23.254.164.92:8000/update/49890878) from the article; Microsoft and StepSecurity independently list this as the stage-2 download endpoint, so a hit is near-certainly the dropper. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised-using-easy-day-js
ATT&CKT1105 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/sandbox detonation of the sample making the same fetch
  • A blue-team connectivity test confirming the IOC is reachable/blocked
  • Shared NAT egress where another tool coincidentally targets the same /24 (verify exact IP+port)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess — a node.exe/npm child reaching this IP confirms dropper execution; capture the host, user, and the resolved second-stage file in %TEMP%. 2) Contain: block 23.254.164.92 at the egress firewall, isolate the host, and treat as credential+wallet compromise (rotate dev/cloud/npm tokens, browser secrets). 3) Hunt: from the same host pivot to 23.254.164.123 beacons and C:\ProgramData\NodePackages persistence; block the full 23.254.164.0/24 Hostwinds range pending review.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "23.254.164.92" and RemotePort == 8000
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "23.254.164.92" and DstPortNumber == 8000
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cross-platform stealer RAT C2 beacon to 23.254.164.123 AICommand & Control High
Hunts the second-stage crypto-stealer/RAT beaconing to its C2 at 23.254.164.123 roughly every 10 minutes over a self-signed wolfSSL channel. Aggregates repeat connections per host to surface the sustained beacon cadence rather than a single hit, distinguishing it from the one-shot dropper download. Rationale: Anchors on the article's RAT C2 IP (23.254.164.123) and the ~10-minute beacon described; the count>=3 aggregation captures the sustained cadence and filters single stray probes. No Sigma emitted because the detection is a threshold/aggregation, not a single-event shape. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.mend.io/blog/mastra-npm-scope-takeover-easy-day-js/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sandbox/IR detonation of the stealer producing repeat beacons
  • Security tooling actively probing the IOC for reachability
  • Another host in the same /24 being contacted for unrelated reasons (pin to exact IP)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm beacon cadence and the originating process; a ~10-min periodic connection from a non-browser process is the RAT. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block 23.254.164.123 at egress, and snapshot memory before reimage; treat all secrets entered on the host as compromised. 3) Hunt: enumerate persistence (C:\ProgramData\NodePackages on Windows, ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.nvm.protocal.plist on macOS, ~/.config/systemd/user/nvmconf.service on Linux) and check other hosts beaconing to the same /24.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP == "23.254.164.123"
| summarize ConnCount=count(), BeaconHours=dcount(bin(Timestamp, 1h)),
            FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp),
            Ports=make_set(RemotePort, 5), Proc=any(InitiatingProcessFileName)
            by DeviceName, RemoteIP
| where ConnCount >= 3   // >=3 hits = repeat beacon, not a stray probe
| order by ConnCount desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr == "23.254.164.123"
| summarize ConnCount=count(), BeaconHours=dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)),
            FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated),
            Ports=make_set(DstPortNumber, 5) by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr
| where ConnCount >= 3   // >=3 hits = repeat beacon, not a stray probe
| order by ConnCount desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationIp:23.254.164.123
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4="23.254.164.123"
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
| count >= 3
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count dc(_time) as distinct_times min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_ip="23.254.164.123" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where count >= 3 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count dc(_time) as distinct_times min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_ip="23.254.164.123" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where count >= 3 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
easy-day-js stealer persistence masquerading as Node tooling (NodePackages / LaunchAgent / systemd) AIInstallation High
Hunts the cross-platform persistence the stealer installs while disguised as Node tooling: Windows staging under C:\ProgramData\NodePackages, macOS LaunchAgent com.nvm.protocal.plist, and Linux systemd user service nvmconf.service. Article-specific because these exact persistence names are unique to this campaign. Rationale: Uses the three campaign-unique persistence names from the article (C:\ProgramData\NodePackages, com.nvm.protocal.plist, nvmconf.service) — the misspelled 'protocal' and 'nvmconf' are distinctive enough that a hit is effectively a true positive. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.kodemsecurity.com/resources/mastra-npm-packages-compromised-easy-day-js-supply-chain-attack-iocs-and-response-runbook
ATT&CKT1543.001 T1543.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal tool coincidentally writing to C:\ProgramData\NodePackages (verify against the exact plist/service names)
  • Restored backup re-creating a previously-quarantined persistence file
  • IR responder copying the artifact for analysis
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the persistence file content points to a NodePackages-staged payload or beacon; capture the writing process. 2) Contain: remove the LaunchAgent/systemd unit/Run entry, kill the persisted process, isolate the host, and rotate all credentials/wallets used there. 3) Hunt: correlate with 23.254.164.92/.123 traffic and the easy-day-js install artifacts on the same and peer hosts; sweep all OS types since persistence is cross-platform.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @"\ProgramData\NodePackages" or FileName in~ ("com.nvm.protocal.plist","nvmconf.service")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has @"\ProgramData\NodePackages" or TargetFileName in~ ("com.nvm.protocal.plist","nvmconf.service")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Mastra easy-day-js second-stage stealer payload by SHA256 AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the obfuscated cross-platform crypto-stealer/RAT second stage by file hash on both write and execution. Hash matching is resilient to IP/infra rotation and is effectively zero-FP; the primary hash (221c45...) is the article-named stage-2 payload corroborated by Microsoft. Rationale: Primary hash 221c45a7... is the article-named second-stage payload and is corroborated by Microsoft Threat Intelligence; the additional campaign hashes are bundled IOCs. Hash matching is zero-FP and survives infrastructure rotation, complementing the IP-based UCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://socket.dev/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis/sandbox host where the sample was intentionally executed
  • EDR/AV quarantine copy retaining the hash on disk
  • Threat-intel platform caching the sample for enrichment
Response runbook
1) Triage: any hit is high-confidence malicious — confirm host, user, and whether the hash was written vs executed; the payload self-deletes, so a FileWrite without a later process may indicate cleanup. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture memory, and treat as full credential+wallet compromise — rotate cloud/npm/dev secrets and assume browser-stored wallet data exfiltrated. 3) Hunt: pivot from the host to 23.254.164.92/.123 traffic and NodePackages/LaunchAgent/systemd persistence; submit the hash to org-wide retro-hunt across EDR.

union
( DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SHA256 in (payloadHashes)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Kind="FileWrite", Path=FolderPath, Name=FileName, SHA256,
            Proc=InitiatingProcessFileName, Cmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine ),
( DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SHA256 in (payloadHashes)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Kind="ProcExec", Path=FolderPath, Name=FileName, SHA256,
            Proc=InitiatingProcessFileName, Cmd=ProcessCommandLine )
| order by Timestamp desc
let payloadHashes = dynamic(["221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf","b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4","c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638","cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066","9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileSHA256 in (payloadHashes)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("23.254.164.92", "23.254.164.123") or RemoteUrl has_any ("hwsrv-1327786.hostwindsdns.com", "hwsrv-1327785.hostwindsdns.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["23.254.164.92", "23.254.164.123"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["hwsrv-1327786.hostwindsdns.com", "hwsrv-1327785.hostwindsdns.com"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain

description: |

    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.

date: 2026/05/02
tags:

Suspicious browser extension installation Installation Medium
Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.
ATT&CKT1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry DeviceRegistryEvents
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any ("\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\","\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\","\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey,
          RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Browser Extension Installation via Registry
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0a
status: experimental
description: |
    Registry writes under the browser extension policy keys —
    administrative install of an extension. Often used by adware /
    info-stealers to bypass user-level extension controls.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1176/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1176
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    category: registry_event
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetObject|contains:
            - '\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Group-policy-managed extension whitelists
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry
    where (Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\*")
    by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.registry_value_name, Registry.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry
    where (Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\*")
    by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.registry_value_name, Registry.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

title: Crypto-Wallet Keystore Access by Non-Wallet Process
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d02
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers / wallet drainers read keystore files from MetaMask,
    Exodus, Atomic, Phantom, Bitcoin, Electrum, Ethereum-cli wallets.
    Filtering out the legitimate wallet binaries leaves only attacker
    activity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1005/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1005
    - attack.collection
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Ethereum\keystore\'
            - '\Bitcoin\'
            - '\Exodus\'
            - '\Electrum\wallets\'
            - '\MetaMask\'
            - '\Phantom\'
            - '\Atomic\Local Storage\'
    filter_legit:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\MetaMask.exe'
            - '\Exodus.exe'
            - '\Atomic.exe'
            - '\electrum.exe'
            - '\Bitcoin.exe'
            - '\Phantom.exe'
    condition: selection_path and not filter_legit
falsepositives:
    - Backup software
level: high

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Bitcoin\wallet.dat"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Exodus\exodus.wallet*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Electrum\wallets\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\MetaMask\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Phantom\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Atomic\Local Storage\*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe","electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Ethereum\keystore\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Bitcoin\wallet.dat"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Exodus\exodus.wallet*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Electrum\wallets\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\MetaMask\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Phantom\*"

PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")

SecurityEvent

// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.

        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9") or SHA1 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9") or MD5 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9") or SHA1 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9") or MD5 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9")

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)

        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,

                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Unauthenticated POST to LobeHub /webapi/proxy (CVE-2026-54157 SSRF exploitation) · [LLM] Browser-driven CSRF to LobeHub /webapi/proxy with cross-origin Referer (cookie injection / session fixation) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-54157: LobeHub: Unauthenticated SSRF in `/webapi/prox
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Unauthenticated POST to LobeHub /webapi/proxy (CVE-2026-54157 SSRF exploitation) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound POST requests to the unauthenticated /webapi/proxy route on a self-hosted LobeHub (@lobehub/lobehub <= 2.1.56) instance — the only webapi route missing checkAuth(). Filters to requests lacking a Clerk __session cookie, which is the discriminator between attacker SSRF abuse and legitimate authenticated client-side URL previews. Rationale: Uses the article's exact vulnerable route (/webapi/proxy), POST method, and the Clerk __session cookie name as the auth discriminator — legitimate previews are authenticated, SSRF abuse is not, matching the advisory's 'only webapi route missing checkAuth()' detail. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@lobehub/lobehub/CVE-2026-54157/ • https://app.opencve.io/cve/?vendor=lobehub • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mxhq-xw3g-rphc
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate LobeHub client-side URL-preview feature making proxy calls without a session in unauthenticated/anonymous configs
  • Vulnerability scanners (e.g. Nuclei templates for CVE-2026-54157) probing the endpoint
  • Uptime/health-check monitors hitting /webapi/proxy
  • Authorized pentest or post-patch validation traffic
Suppression filter
| where HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has_any ("Nuclei","masscan","zgrab","Expanse","nmap")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all matching SrcIpAddr, inspect the proxied target URLs/body if WAF captured them; check whether source IPs are internal app traffic, known scanners, or external/unknown. 2) Contain: if instance is <= 2.1.56, upgrade @lobehub/lobehub to >= 2.1.57 (adds checkAuth() to the route) or block POST /webapi/proxy at the WAF; expire any Clerk sessions issued during the window. 3) Hunt: review egress from the LobeHub host for SSRF callbacks to internal ranges, cloud metadata (169.254.169.254), or Vercel management plane, and check for reflected Set-Cookie abuse.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod == "POST"
| where Url has "/webapi/proxy"
// legitimate client previews carry the Clerk __session cookie; SSRF abuse does not
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderCookie) or HttpRequestHeaderCookie !has "__session"
| summarize Requests=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), UserAgents=make_set(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent,5), SampleUrls=make_set(Url,5) by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname
| order by Requests desc

Browser-driven CSRF to LobeHub /webapi/proxy with cross-origin Referer (cookie injection / session fixation) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts egress web-proxy traffic from corporate browsers POSTing to app.lobehub.com/webapi/proxy where the Referer is cross-origin (not lobehub.com) — the signature of the CSRF auto-submit form that abuses reflected Set-Cookie headers to inject __session/__clerk_db_jwt cookies and fix a victim's Clerk session. Legitimate LobeHub link previews always carry a same-site lobehub.com Referer. Rationale: Built from the advisory's CSRF PoC (auto-submitting form POST to https://app.lobehub.com/webapi/proxy with enctype text/plain) and the reflected __session/__clerk_db_jwt cookie names; the cross-origin Referer is the high-fidelity discriminator versus the app's same-site preview calls. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@lobehub/lobehub/CVE-2026-54157/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mxhq-xw3g-rphc
ATT&CKT1190 T1539
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Browser Referrer-Policy: no-referrer or privacy extensions stripping the Referer on legitimate same-site preview POSTs
  • Proxy/SWG not capturing the Referer header, leaving it blank
  • LobeHub embedded in a sanctioned internal portal/iframe on a non-lobehub.com host
  • Users accessing LobeHub via a custom corporate domain that fronts app.lobehub.com
Suppression filter
| where isnotempty(Referer) and Referer has "://"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the SrcUsername/SrcIpAddr and the cross-origin Referer host — pivot on that host to find the malicious page that auto-submitted the form. 2) Contain: force re-authentication / invalidate Clerk sessions for the affected user(s), block the attacker Referer domain at the SWG, and warn users not to revisit it; coordinate with LobeHub if SaaS. 3) Hunt: search for follow-on logins to lobehub.com using the same fixed __session value, and review the same users for other CSRF-style cross-origin POSTs to sensitive endpoints.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod == "POST"
| where Url has "app.lobehub.com/webapi/proxy"
| extend Referer = tostring(HttpRequestHeaderReferer)
// genuine in-app previews referer from lobehub.com; CSRF auto-submit referer is the attacker page (or absent)
| where Referer !has "lobehub.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, Referer, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

let LookbackDays = 7d;

Crawl4AI /screenshot or /pdf output_path traversal → arbitrary file write outside output dir AIInstallation High
Hunts the CWE-22 arbitrary-file-write in Crawl4AI's /screenshot and /pdf endpoints, where an unvalidated output_path lets an attacker drop files outside /tmp/crawl4ai-outputs. Detects the crawl4ai server process (python/uvicorn/gunicorn) creating files in sensitive locations (cron, .ssh, shell rc files, /etc, /root) it should never write to. Rationale: Anchored on the article's named endpoints (/screenshot, /pdf), the named safe directory (/tmp/crawl4ai-outputs), and the server process identity. A web crawler writing to cron/.ssh/.bashrc is near-zero-FP. Datadog left empty — provided linux.auditd schema lacks a target-file-path field. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/GHSA-365w-hqf6-vxfg/ • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/crawl4ai-docker-api-local-file-inclusion-via-file-url-handling
ATT&CKT1190 T1053.003 T1098.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Crawl4AI configured with a custom CRAWL4AI_OUTPUT_DIR pointing at /app or /usr/local (operator misconfig)
  • Admin/CI process running inside the container as the same python interpreter doing legitimate package installs into /usr/local
  • Browser engine (chromium) writing cache under /home/appuser/.cache if process attribution rolls up to python
  • Init/entrypoint scripts seeding config into /app on first boot
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath startswith "/usr/local/lib/python" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip","setup.py","wheel"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full FolderPath/FileName and the InitiatingProcessCommandLine — confirm the write landed outside /tmp/crawl4ai-outputs and inspect the dropped file's content (web shell, cron entry, authorized_keys). Correlate with web logs for the /screenshot or /pdf request carrying output_path. 2) Contain: isolate the container/host, kill the crawl4ai worker, and revoke any keys/creds present in the written path; if a cron or authorized_keys entry was added, remove it. 3) Hunt: search all crawl4ai hosts for other writes outside the output dir, and pivot on the source IP across /screenshot, /pdf, /execute_js. Upgrade Crawl4AI to >=0.8.7.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)^(python[0-9.]*|uvicorn|gunicorn)$"
| where FolderPath !startswith "/tmp/crawl4ai-outputs"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/etc/","/root/","/etc/cron","/.ssh","authorized_keys","/.bashrc","/.profile","/usr/local/","/app/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)(python|uvicorn|gunicorn)"
| where TargetFilePath !startswith "/tmp/crawl4ai-outputs"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/","/root/","/etc/cron","/.ssh","authorized_keys","/.bashrc","/.profile","/usr/local/","/app/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Crawl4AI SSRF: crawler process reaching cloud-metadata or RFC1918 internal IPs AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the SSRF chain across Crawl4AI's /crawl, /md, /llm, /execute_js and webhook endpoints (CWE-918), where attacker-supplied URLs make the server fetch internal services and the 169.254.169.254 cloud-metadata endpoint — including the IPv6-mapped bypass (CVE-2026-53754). Flags the crawl4ai/browser process connecting to metadata or private ranges, which a public-web crawler should never do. Rationale: Cloud-metadata IP 169.254.169.254 (and its ::ffff: mapped form, the CVE-2026-53754 bypass) is essentially never a legitimate destination for a public-web crawler, making it a high-fidelity SSRF anchor; RFC1918 hits are the broader hunting tier. Process-scoped to the named crawl4ai runtimes. CloudWatch left empty — IMDS access is host-network, not visible in CloudTrail. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/GHSA-365w-hqf6-vxfg/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/CVE-2026-53754/
ATT&CKT1190 T1552.005 T1046
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Crawl4AI legitimately connecting to an internal Redis (6379) / Postgres (5432) backend on the Docker bridge network
  • Crawl4AI calling a self-hosted LLM/embedding endpoint on a private IP (Ollama, vLLM)
  • Health-check or service-mesh sidecar traffic from the same container to private ranges
  • Crawling an explicitly allowed internal staging site during QA
Suppression filter
| where not (RemotePort in (6379, 5432, 11434) and not MetadataHit)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the destination — a hit on 169.254.169.254 is a confirmed SSRF/credential-theft attempt; for RFC1918 hits, check RemotePort/RemoteUrl and whether it matches a known internal service. Pull the matching /crawl, /md, /llm or webhook request from web logs. 2) Contain: if metadata was reached, rotate the instance role / IMDS credentials immediately and enforce IMDSv2 (hop limit 1); block the source IP and disable /execute_js (CRAWL4AI_EXECUTE_JS_ENABLED). 3) Hunt: review CloudTrail/Activity logs for any API calls made with the instance role shortly after the metadata hit, and pivot on the source IP for internal-range fan-out (port scanning). Upgrade to >=0.8.7.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)^(python[0-9.]*|uvicorn|gunicorn|chromium|chrome|headless_shell|node)$"
| extend MetadataHit = (RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254" or RemoteIP == "::ffff:169.254.169.254")
| where MetadataHit or ipv4_is_private(RemoteIP) or ipv4_is_in_range(RemoteIP, "169.254.0.0/16")
| extend Severity = iff(MetadataHit, "CRITICAL-cloud-metadata", "internal-SSRF")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Severity
| order by Severity asc, Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr == "169.254.169.254" or DstIpAddr == "::ffff:169.254.169.254" or ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) or ipv4_is_in_range(DstIpAddr, "169.254.0.0/16")
| where DstPortNumber in (80, 443, 8000, 8080) or NetworkApplicationProtocol has_any ("http","https")
| extend Severity = iff(DstIpAddr == "169.254.169.254" or DstIpAddr == "::ffff:169.254.169.254", "CRITICAL-cloud-metadata", "internal-SSRF")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Severity
| order by Severity asc, TimeGenerated desc

Crawl4AI /execute_js sandbox escape: crawler/browser process spawning a shell AIExploitation High
Hunts the arbitrary-JavaScript-execution / hook-sandbox-escape vulnerability (CWE-94) in Crawl4AI's /execute_js endpoint, where attacker JS (or the asyncio/hook bypass) breaks out to OS command execution. Detects the python/uvicorn/gunicorn server or its headless-chromium/node children spawning an interactive shell — behaviour a web crawler never exhibits. Rationale: Process-tree pivot on the article's named runtime (python/uvicorn/gunicorn + the playwright headless-chromium it drives) spawning a shell directly maps the /execute_js RCE and hook sandbox-escape outcome. Datadog left empty — the provided linux.auditd schema exposes no parent-process field, so the parent→child constraint cannot be expressed. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/GHSA-365w-hqf6-vxfg/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/CVE-2026-53754/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Crawl4AI legitimately shelling out to a PDF/image post-processing tool (wkhtmltopdf, ghostscript) via subprocess
  • Container entrypoint or healthcheck script invoking sh from the gunicorn master
  • Operator running 'docker exec ... bash' attributed to the server process tree
  • A debugging hook intentionally enabled in non-prod that runs shell commands
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("wkhtmltopdf","ghostscript","/usr/bin/gs","libreoffice") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child ProcessCommandLine — benign post-processing (ghostscript/wkhtmltopdf) vs reverse shell / curl|sh / recon (id, uname, whoami). Correlate timing with a POST to /execute_js in web logs. 2) Contain: kill the shell and parent worker, isolate the container, and disable /execute_js via CRAWL4AI_EXECUTE_JS_ENABLED=false (and remove --disable-web-security if present). 3) Hunt: from the same host pivot to UC2 (SSRF egress) and UC1 (file writes), and search DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound C2 from the shell PID. Upgrade to >=0.8.7.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)^(python[0-9.]*|uvicorn|gunicorn|node|chromium|chrome|headless_shell)$"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ash","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)/(python[0-9.]*|uvicorn|gunicorn|node|chromium|chrome|headless_shell)$"
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)/(sh|bash|dash|zsh|ash)$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Crawl4AI unauthenticated access to /monitor endpoints (auth bypass) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the CWE-306 missing-authentication flaw where Crawl4AI's monitor router was mounted without token_dep, exposing destructive endpoints like /monitor/actions/cleanup and the /monitor/ws WebSocket with no auth. Detects successful requests to /monitor paths that carry no Authorization header. Rationale: Uses the article's exact vulnerable paths (/monitor/actions/cleanup, /monitor/ws) plus the auth-bypass signature — a successful response with an empty Authorization header. Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch left empty: this needs HTTP request-header visibility that only the reverse-proxy/WAF (Sentinel ImWebSession / CIM Web) carries; Sigma skipped because 'webserver' is outside the allowed logsource categories. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/GHSA-365w-hqf6-vxfg/
ATT&CKT1190 T1485
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal monitoring/uptime check polling /monitor without a token (pre-patch, by design)
  • An ops dashboard reverse-proxy that strips the Authorization header before the app tier (header invisible to upstream logger)
  • Health probes from Kubernetes/Docker hitting /monitor/* and returning 200
  • Internal load-balancer keep-alive traffic to the monitor WebSocket
Suppression filter
| where not (SrcIpAddr in ("127.0.0.1","::1") or HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has_any ("kube-probe","ELB-HealthChecker","Datadog","Pingdom"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the request reached a destructive endpoint (/monitor/actions/cleanup) vs read-only monitor views, and whether the source IP is internal/expected. Check for a burst of /monitor/* enumeration from one IP. 2) Contain: put the monitor router behind auth (deploy >=0.8.7 / set CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN) and restrict network access to the Docker API; block the offending source IP at the proxy. 3) Hunt: from the same source IP, pivot to /screenshot, /pdf, /execute_js and /crawl activity (UC1/UC2/UC3/UC5) and review whether cleanup actually deleted job/output data.

| where Url has_any ("/monitor/actions/cleanup","/monitor/actions","/monitor/ws","/monitor/")
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)
| where HttpStatusCode in ("200","101","204")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Crawl4AI web-payload abuse: path traversal, XSS, file:// and metadata-IP in crawl requests AIDelivery Medium
Hunts malicious payloads sent to Crawl4AI's exposed endpoints (/screenshot, /pdf, /crawl, /md, /llm, /execute_js, /markdown_extraction, /llm_extraction): output_path traversal sequences, stored-XSS markup (CWE-79), file:// LFI URLs, and literal cloud-metadata / IPv6-mapped targets used for SSRF. A single web-log pivot that surfaces exploitation attempts before they succeed. Rationale: Combines the article's full endpoint inventory with concrete exploit signatures it names: output_path traversal, XSS markup, the file:// LFI vector (VulnCheck-confirmed) and the ::ffff: IPv6-mapped metadata bypass (CVE-2026-53754). Hunting tier because many payloads ride in POST bodies that not all proxies log into the URL field — pairs with the behavioural UCs (1/2/3) for confirmation. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-365w-hqf6-vxfg • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/CVE-2026-53754/ • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/crawl4ai-docker-api-local-file-inclusion-via-file-url-handling
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate crawl target whose URL genuinely contains '../' in its query string or path
  • Security scanners / pentest tooling (Burp, Nuclei) probing the endpoints during authorized testing
  • A crawled page URL that legitimately references file:// in a parameter value
  • Crawling a security blog whose URL contains '<script' or 'onerror=' as article-content text
Suppression filter
| where not (HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has_any ("Nuclei","Burp","sqlmap","Nessus") or SrcIpAddr in ("127.0.0.1","::1"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: classify the payload type (traversal vs XSS vs file:// vs metadata-IP) and check the HTTP status — a 200 on /screenshot+output_path traversal or /crawl+file:// suggests success. Cross-reference the source IP with UC1/UC2/UC3 host telemetry for an actual file write, SSRF egress, or shell. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the proxy/WAF, disable /execute_js, and ensure the patched SSRF/path validators are deployed (>=0.8.7). 3) Hunt: enumerate every distinct payload that IP sent across all endpoints, and confirm whether any stored XSS persisted in the monitor dashboard (escapeHtml present?).
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
