Crawl4AI CVE-2026-53753 sandbox-escape payload (gi_frame/f_back/f_builtins) in POST /crawl body AIExploitation High
Hunts unauthenticated exploitation of the Crawl4AI Docker API AST sandbox escape by matching the frame-introspection chain (gi_frame, f_back, f_builtins, __import__) inside a JsonCssExtractionStrategy computed-field expression POSTed to /crawl. These Python generator/frame attribute names have zero benign reason to appear in crawl-extraction schemas, making them a high-fidelity exploit signature. Rationale: Uses the article's verbatim exploit primitives gi_frame/f_back/f_builtins/__import__ plus the JsonCssExtractionStrategy schema key and the /crawl endpoint. The frame-attribute chain is the literal sandbox-escape technique named by the advisory and has no benign occurrence in extraction schemas. Cross-checked against the GitLab Advisory Database (CVSS 9.8, fixed 0.8.7) which confirms the gi_frame.f_back computed-field eval() escape. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/CVE-2026-53753/ • https://github.com/unclecode/crawl4ai/security
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanners / pentest tooling (Nuclei, Burp) replaying the public PoC against an internal Crawl4AI instance during authorised testing
  • Internal red-team validation of the patch on a staging Crawl4AI container
  • A developer pasting the advisory PoC into a request while reproducing the bug for the 0.8.7 upgrade
  • WAF that mirrors blocked-request bodies into the same log index (action=blocked rows — still worth reviewing but not a live compromise)
Suppression filter
| where DeviceAction !in~ ("blocked","denied","reset")  // keep only requests that actually reached the app; drop WAF-blocked replays during triage tuning
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request for the SourceIP+RequestClientApplication; confirm the body carries a gi_frame/f_back chain inside a JsonCssExtractionStrategy schema, and check the running Crawl4AI version (<=0.8.6 vulnerable) and whether CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN/JWT auth is set. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the WAF, remove the container from public network exposure, and rotate any secrets the container can reach (env vars, mounted files, instance role). 3) Hunt: on the affected host run the post-RCE process-tree and credential-enumeration detections from first-seen time, and review egress from the uvicorn/python process to attacker infrastructure.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/crawl"
| where Message has_any ("gi_frame","f_back","f_builtins","JsonCssExtractionStrategy","__import__")
   or RequestContext has_any ("gi_frame","f_back","f_builtins","__import__")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, DeviceAction, RequestClientApplication, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
(sourcetype="*nginx*" OR sourcetype="*apache*" OR sourcetype="*waf*" OR sourcetype="*proxy*") "/crawl" ("gi_frame" OR "f_back" OR "f_builtins" OR "JsonCssExtractionStrategy" OR "__import__")
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by host, source, sourcetype, clientip
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - count
Crawl4AI/uvicorn post-RCE: Python web service spawning shell or recon binaries AIInstallation High
Hunts the post-exploitation footprint of CVE-2026-53753: the Crawl4AI Python/uvicorn/gunicorn process spawning interactive shells (sh, bash, dash) or reconnaissance utilities (curl, wget, nc, socat, whoami, id, uname). A crawler web service has no legitimate reason to fork these, so this is a high-confidence signal that the AST sandbox escape achieved code execution. Rationale: Anchors on the article's stated impact ('execute arbitrary system commands') by pivoting on the exact server stack named in the advisory (Crawl4AI Docker API served by uvicorn/Python) spawning shells or recon tools — a tree that never occurs in normal crawler operation. The pip/pytest/playwright exclusion strips the only routine python-spawns-shell cases. Corroborated via GitLab GLAD entry for CVE-2026-53753. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/CVE-2026-53753/ • https://github.com/unclecode/crawl4ai/security
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Container build/CI steps where python runs 'pip install' which forks sh (covered by the filter)
  • Crawl4AI/Playwright bootstrapping that shells out to install browser dependencies on first run
  • A devops entrypoint script that uses python to wrap curl/wget for healthchecks
  • Operator debugging the container interactively via 'docker exec' producing python->bash (verify it was a human shell, not the web worker)
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install","-m pip","setup.py","pytest","jupyter","playwright install","conda")) and AccountName !in~ ("root")  // optionally drop root-context build steps if the service runs as a non-root crawl user
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child command line and the parent uvicorn/python tree; confirm this is the Crawl4AI web worker (not a CI/pip/playwright bootstrap or an interactive docker exec). 2) Contain: isolate the container/host from the network, kill the offending process tree, and snapshot the container filesystem and memory for IR. 3) Hunt: pivot to the /crawl WAF detection to find the originating exploit request, and to the credential-enumeration detection to see whether secrets or the metadata endpoint were touched; review all egress from the worker process.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","nc","ncat","netcat","socat","whoami","id","uname")
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install","-m pip","setup.py","pytest","jupyter","playwright install"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where TargetProcessName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","nc","ncat","netcat","socat","whoami","id","uname")
| where not(TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install","setup.py","pytest","jupyter","playwright install"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Crawl4AI post-RCE credential & cloud-metadata enumeration via Python-spawned subprocess AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts post-exploitation credential theft following CVE-2026-53753: a Crawl4AI Python/shell process reading /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, the process environment (/proc/self/environ, printenv), or the cloud instance metadata service (169.254.169.254). The advisory explicitly calls out 'exfiltrate secrets', and a web crawler reaching these paths is a strong indicator the sandbox escape was used to harvest credentials. Rationale: Grounded in the advisory's 'read/write files, and exfiltrate secrets' impact statement and the listed T1552.001 technique. Anchors the well-known secret targets (/etc/shadow, /etc/passwd, /proc/self/environ, IMDS 169.254.169.254) to the Crawl4AI Python/shell parent chain so it fires on attacker harvesting rather than routine admin reads. Corroborated via the GitLab Advisory Database entry for CVE-2026-53753. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/CVE-2026-53753/ • https://github.com/unclecode/crawl4ai/security
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.005 T1083 T1082
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A container entrypoint/healthcheck script reading /etc/passwd to resolve a uid before dropping privileges
  • Legitimate app code calling printenv/env for config diagnostics under the python worker
  • Monitoring agents (Datadog/aws-otel) querying 169.254.169.254 for instance identity — verify the parent is the agent, not the crawl worker
  • An operator running 'cat /etc/passwd' via docker exec while troubleshooting (interactive, not web-worker-spawned)
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("datadog-agent","aws-otel-collector","cloud-init")) and not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("getent passwd","id -u"))  // drop monitoring agents and benign uid lookups while keeping shadow/environ/IMDS reads
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify which secret was touched (/etc/shadow vs environ vs IMDS) and confirm the parent chain traces to the Crawl4AI uvicorn/python worker rather than a sidecar/monitoring agent; check whether 169.254.169.254 actually returned IAM/role credentials. 2) Contain: rotate every credential reachable from the container — env-var secrets, mounted files, and any cloud instance-profile/role credentials — and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: in CloudTrail, search for AssumeRole and API activity using the container's instance-profile role from new source IPs since first-seen, and pivot to the /crawl exploit and shell-spawn detections to scope the full intrusion.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn","sh","bash","dash")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/shadow","/etc/passwd","/proc/self/environ","/proc/self/cmdline","169.254.169.254","latest/meta-data")
   or FileName in~ ("printenv","env")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn","sh","bash","dash")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/shadow","/etc/passwd","/proc/self/environ","/proc/self/cmdline","169.254.169.254","latest/meta-data")
   or TargetProcessName in~ ("printenv","env")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

JetBrains IDE plugin AI-key exfil: endpoint egress to C2 39.107.60.51 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts any host making an outbound connection to the hardcoded attacker C2 39.107.60.51 used by 15 trojanized JetBrains Marketplace plugins (DeepSeek/CodeGPT clones) to ship stolen OpenAI/DeepSeek/SiliconFlow API keys. The connection is initiated by the JetBrains IDE JVM the instant a user clicks Apply on the plugin settings, so the process context is a Java/JetBrains runtime, not a browser. Rationale: Anchored on the single hardcoded C2 IP 39.107.60.51 (verbatim from the article's network-call code block, defanged 39.107.60[.]51) — a dedicated attacker host with no legitimate use, cross-confirmed by BleepingComputer and The Hacker News. Any connection is dispositive. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/malicious-jetbrains-marketplace-plugins-steal-ai-api-keys-from-developers/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/malicious-jetbrains-plugins-steal-ai.html • https://blog.jetbrains.com/platform/2026/06/marketplace-ecosystem-security-update-malicious-ai-plugins/
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher/sandbox detonating one of the named plugins to reproduce the IOC
  • Threat-intel or attack-surface scanners (Shodan/Censys) probing the IP from a corporate egress
  • IP reuse: the Alibaba Cloud address later reassigned to a benign tenant (validate WHOIS/first-seen date)
  • A SOAR/enrichment playbook auto-resolving or pinging the IOC and generating an event
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the InitiatingProcess is a JetBrains runtime (idea64.exe/pycharm64.exe/java/jetbrains-runtime) and pull the user; enumerate that user's installed JetBrains plugins against the 15 named IDs. 2) Contain: treat every AI provider API key (OpenAI/DeepSeek/SiliconFlow) entered on that host as compromised — revoke and rotate immediately, uninstall the plugin, and block 39.107.60.51 at egress. 3) Hunt: sweep DeviceNetworkEvents org-wide for the IP, and pivot to UC 'malicious JetBrains plugin install' to find dormant infections that haven't yet phoned home.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "39.107.60.51"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "39.107.60.51"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceHostName,
          SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL,
          ApplicationProtocol, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc

JetBrains AI-key stealer HTTP exfil: cleartext POST to /api/software/ path AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the application-layer signature of the theft in web-proxy/network-sensor telemetry: a plaintext HTTP POST to the URI path /api/software/<name> carrying the victim's API key as JSON. This survives C2 IP rotation by keying on the distinctive hardcoded URL path, and catches IDE traffic that egresses through a proxy where EDR socket attribution is weak. Rationale: Uses two verbatim article strings — the URL path /api/software/ from the network-call code block and the C2 IP 39.107.60.51 — over plaintext HTTP (article: 'reached over plain HTTP'). The path keys the detection independently of the IP. Datadog/Falcon left empty: standard FDR network events and the listed Datadog sources don't carry HTTP URI paths, so this needs proxy/web-gateway telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/malicious-jetbrains-marketplace-plugins-steal-ai-api-keys-from-developers/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/fifteen-jetbrains-marketplace/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An internal/SaaS API that legitimately exposes a '/api/software/' inventory endpoint reached over HTTP
  • Software-asset-management or patch agents POSTing to a vendor '/api/software/' path
  • Web-app vulnerability scanners fuzzing '/api/' routes from a corporate host
  • Proxy replay/cached events double-counting the same flow
Suppression filter
| where DstIpAddr == "39.107.60.51" or Url has "39.107.60.51/api/software/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the full request — confirm the host header/destination resolves to 39.107.60.51 and, if PCAP/full-proxy is available, look for the static header X-Api-Key: F48D2AA7CF341F782C1D and a JSON body containing an 'sk-' key. 2) Contain: rotate/revoke the leaked provider key(s), remove the offending JetBrains plugin, and add both the IP and the URI path as egress-block + proxy-deny rules. 3) Hunt: search proxy logs for any other host hitting /api/software/ (catches infections after a C2 IP change) and correlate with the endpoint-egress UC.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "HttpConnectionInspected"
| where RemoteUrl has "/api/software/" or RemoteUrl has "39.107.60.51"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (Url has "/api/software/" or DstIpAddr == "39.107.60.51")
| where HttpMethod == "POST"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber,
          Url, HttpMethod, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DvcHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious JetBrains Marketplace plugin install (15 DeepSeek/CodeGPT clone IDs) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts on-disk presence or install of any of the 15 trojanized JetBrains plugins by matching their Marketplace display names under a JetBrains \plugins\ directory. Covers the initial-access/supply-chain step and surfaces dormant infections on hosts that haven't yet entered an API key or phoned home to the C2. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim list of 15 malicious plugin display names installed under JetBrains \plugins\ paths — the supply-chain delivery artifact. Hunting-tier because the 'CodeGPT AI Assistant' clone name overlaps the legitimate CodeGPT plugin, so matches need confirmation (pair with the C2-egress UC). Cross-checked against: • https://blog.jetbrains.com/platform/2026/06/marketplace-ecosystem-security-update-malicious-ai-plugins/ • https://hackread.com/malicious-jetbrains-plugins-steal-deepseek-openai-api-keys/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • The legitimate 'CodeGPT' plugin (genuine vendor) whose folder name substring overlaps the malicious 'CodeGPT AI Assistant' clone
  • Developers who installed an affected plugin before JetBrains' takedown and have since updated/removed it (stale on-disk artifact)
  • Security team deliberately installing a sample for analysis in a lab VM
  • JetBrains Marketplace cache/temp extraction folders retaining the plugin name after backend disable
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe") and FolderPath !has "\\Marketplace\\cache\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the exact plugin ID inside the matched folder's plugin.xml against the 15 known IDs (e.g. org.sm.yms.toolkit, com.my.code.tools, ord.cp.code.ai.kit) — this disambiguates the malicious 'CodeGPT AI Assistant' from the legitimate CodeGPT. 2) Contain: uninstall the plugin, and immediately revoke/rotate any OpenAI/DeepSeek/SiliconFlow API key the developer may have entered (assume compromised even without observed egress). 3) Hunt: pivot every matched host to the C2-egress and HTTP-path UCs for 39.107.60.51 to confirm exfiltration, and query software inventory across the fleet for the remaining plugin IDs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where FolderPath has "JetBrains" and FolderPath has "plugins"
| where FolderPath has_any (
    "DeepSeek Junit Test","DeepSeek Git Commit","DeepSeek FindBugs",
    "DeepSeek AI Chat","DeepSeek Dev AI","DeepSeek AI Coding",
    "AI FindBugs","AI Git Commitor","AI Coder Review","DeepSeek Coder AI",
    "AI Coder Assistant","DeepSeek Code Review","CodeGPT AI Assistant",
    "DeepSeek AI Assist","Coding Simple Tool")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Files=make_set(FileName, 20)
          by DeviceName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where TargetFilePath has "JetBrains" and TargetFilePath has "plugins"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (
    "DeepSeek Junit Test","DeepSeek Git Commit","DeepSeek FindBugs",
    "DeepSeek AI Chat","DeepSeek Dev AI","DeepSeek AI Coding",
    "AI FindBugs","AI Git Commitor","AI Coder Review","DeepSeek Coder AI",
    "AI Coder Assistant","DeepSeek Code Review","CodeGPT AI Assistant",
    "DeepSeek AI Assist","Coding Simple Tool")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

vLLM OpenAI API auth bypass via malformed Host header on /v1/* (CVE-2026-48746) AIExploitation High
Hunts the primary exploit for CVE-2026-48746: a request to a vLLM /v1/* endpoint carrying a Host header that contains URL special characters (/ ? # @), e.g. 'Host: localhost/v1/models?'. The malformed Host poisons Starlette's reconstructed url_path so AuthenticationMiddleware skips the API-key check while FastAPI routing still reaches the protected endpoint. Rationale: Uses the article's exact mechanism (Host header injected with / or ? so reconstructed .path no longer starts with /v1) plus the corroborated PoC value 'localhost/v1/models?' and the /v1/ endpoint family. A legitimate Host header is host[:port] only — any / ? # @ is anomalous, making this very low FP. Cross-checked GHSA-94f4-hr76-p5j6, miggo.io and vLLM docs (default port 8000, /v1/ endpoints). Defender XDR / FDR carry no HTTP-header telemetry, so defender_kql and falcon_logscale_query are empty; Datadog has no generic web-access source in this tenant. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-94f4-hr76-p5j6 • https://www.miggo.io/vulnerability-database/cve/CVE-2026-48746 • https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/serving/openai_compatible_server/
ATT&CKT1190 T1556
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Tenable/Qualys/Nuclei) actively testing CVE-2026-48746 — confirm against scan schedule
  • Penetration testers probing the vLLM endpoint during a sanctioned engagement
  • Broken client SDK that mis-builds base_url and emits a path-laden Host value (rare)
  • Middlebox/SNI rewriter that appends a port or path artifact into the Host header
  • Synthetic monitoring that intentionally fuzzes headers against the API
Suppression filter
| where HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has "kube-probe" and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has "ELB-HealthChecker"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request for the matched SrcIpAddr — confirm the Host header literally contains / or ? and the path is a /v1/ endpoint, and check the response status (a 200/201 means the bypass succeeded). 2) Contain: if not an authorized scanner, block the source IP at the proxy/WAF and place the vLLM instance behind an RFC-conforming proxy (nginx) or upgrade vLLM to >=0.22.0; rotate VLLM_API_KEY. 3) Hunt: from that SrcIpAddr enumerate all /v1/ requests with 200/201 to gauge what model/data was accessed, and pivot on the same Host-header pattern across every other internet-facing vLLM host.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/v1/"                       // vLLM OpenAI-compatible protected endpoints
| where HttpHostName matches regex @"[/?#@]"  // Host header should never contain / ? # @ (e.g. 'localhost/v1/models?')
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, Url, HttpMethod,
          StatusCode = HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent,
          DstHostname, DstPortNumber
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Successful vLLM /v1/* access with no Authorization header (key-bypass outcome, CVE-2026-48746) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the OUTCOME of the auth bypass: a 200/201 response from a vLLM /v1/* endpoint on an instance configured with --api-key / VLLM_API_KEY, where the request carried no Authorization header. On an auth-configured instance this should be impossible; its occurrence indicates the AuthenticationMiddleware was bypassed. Rationale: Targets the article's stated impact verbatim — 'use the API without providing the configured VLLM_API_KEY or --api-key'. ImWebSession.HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization is the only schema field that records header presence, so this is meaningful only on instances where api-key auth IS configured (noted for the analyst). Empty defender/falcon/datadog because none ship HTTP request-header telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-94f4-hr76-p5j6 • https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/serving/openai_compatible_server/
ATT&CKT1556 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • vLLM instance NOT configured with --api-key / VLLM_API_KEY — every request legitimately has no Authorization header (scope this rule to auth-configured hosts only)
  • Reverse proxy terminates auth upstream and strips Authorization before forwarding, so the app log shows no header though the proxy enforced it
  • Intentionally public GET /v1/models used for health/capability discovery
  • Internal monitoring/synthetic checks hitting the API without a key on a non-enforcing listener
  • Localhost/loopback clients where the operator did not require auth
Suppression filter
| where not (Url has "/v1/models" and HttpMethod =~ "GET")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the target vLLM host actually has api-key auth enabled (--api-key / VLLM_API_KEY set); if it does, an unauthenticated 200 on /v1/ is a confirmed bypass. Inspect the Host header on the same request for the / ? # @ signature. 2) Contain: front the instance with an RFC-conforming proxy (nginx) or upgrade to vLLM >=0.22.0, rotate the API key, and restrict /v1/ exposure to trusted networks. 3) Hunt: enumerate every unauthenticated 2xx from that SrcIpAddr (which models/prompts were exercised), then sweep all internet-facing vLLM hosts for the same pattern.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/v1/"                          // vLLM protected OpenAI endpoints
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization) // no API key presented
| where HttpStatusCode in (200, 201)            // but the request still succeeded
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, Url, HttpMethod,
          StatusCode = HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent,
          DstHostname, DstPortNumber
| order by TimeGenerated desc

vLLM auth-bypass probe pattern: 401/403 then 200 on /v1/* from same source (CVE-2026-48746) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the probe-and-exploit sequence against a vLLM instance: the same source IP first receives a 401/403 on a /v1/* endpoint (auth required), then within a short window obtains a 200/201 on /v1/* — consistent with an attacker discovering the API-key requirement and then defeating it via the CVE-2026-48746 Host-header bypass. Rationale: Encodes the attacker workflow implied by the article — the instance enforces a key (401/403 baseline) which is then bypassed (200) — as a same-source temporal correlation, the single biggest noise reducer over a flat 'unauth 200' rule. Surfaces SuccessHost so the analyst can confirm the malformed Host signature on the successful request. Cross-checked GHSA-94f4-hr76-p5j6 and miggo.io. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-94f4-hr76-p5j6 • https://www.miggo.io/vulnerability-database/cve/CVE-2026-48746
ATT&CKT1190 T1556
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate key rotation: a client fails with a stale key (401), the operator updates it, then succeeds (200)
  • Shared NAT / egress gateway makes many distinct users appear as one SrcIpAddr — one fails auth, another succeeds with a valid key
  • Load balancer or proxy that collapses client IPs into a single upstream address
  • Automated client retry after a transient 401 during vLLM startup/model-load races
  • Authorized scanner that records a baseline 401 then re-tests with the bypass payload
Suppression filter
| where SuccessHost matches regex @"[/?#@]"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the SuccessHost field on the matched success event — if it contains / ? # @ the bypass is confirmed, not a key rotation. Verify FailUrl and SuccessUrl hit the same instance. 2) Contain: block the SrcIpAddr, place the instance behind nginx or upgrade vLLM to >=0.22.0, and rotate VLLM_API_KEY. 3) Hunt: pull every /v1/ request from that source post-success to scope model/prompt access, and check whether the same source probed other vLLM hosts in the estate.
let Window = 10m;   // attacker probes auth then bypasses within minutes
let Failures = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where Url has "/v1/"
    | where HttpStatusCode in (401, 403)
    | project FailTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, FailUrl = Url, DstHostname;
let Success = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where Url has "/v1/"
    | where HttpStatusCode in (200, 201)
    | project SuccessTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SuccessUrl = Url, SuccessHost = HttpHostName, DstHostname;
Failures
| join kind=inner Success on SrcIpAddr
| where SuccessTime between (FailTime .. FailTime + Window)
| project FailTime, SuccessTime,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', SuccessTime, FailTime),
          SrcIpAddr, FailUrl, SuccessUrl, SuccessHost, DstHostname
| order by SuccessTime desc

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) as failTime from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*/v1/*" (Web.status=401 OR Web.status=403) by Web.src
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) as successTime from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*/v1/*" (Web.status=200 OR Web.status=201) by Web.src
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| where successTime > failTime AND successTime <= failTime + 600
| eval delaySec = successTime - failTime
| convert ctime(failTime) ctime(successTime)
| table failTime, successTime, delaySec, src
| sort - successTime
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) as failTime from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*/v1/*" (Web.status=401 OR Web.status=403) by Web.src
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) as successTime from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*/v1/*" (Web.status=200 OR Web.status=201) by Web.src

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Langflow unauthenticated RCE: HTTP requests to /api/v1/build_public_tmp public-build endpoint
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Langflow backend (python/uvicorn) spawning OS shell or recon/exfil tool — RCE execution · Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-48519: Langflow: Unauthenticated RCE in Shareable Pla
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Langflow unauthenticated RCE: HTTP requests to /api/v1/build_public_tmp public-build endpoint AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to Langflow's unauthenticated public-flow build route (/api/v1/build_public_tmp/{flow_id}/flow), the exact endpoint CVE-2026-48519 abuses to inject attacker-controlled flow definitions containing arbitrary Python. Surfaces both opportunistic internet scanning and targeted exploitation against exposed Langflow instances (<= 1.9.1). Rationale: Pivots on the exact vulnerable route string '/api/v1/build_public_tmp' named in the advisory PoC cURL — a fixed, non-generic endpoint that only the Shareable Playground build path uses. Hunting tier because legitimate playground users also hit it; triage on source IP and request volume. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/langflow-ai/langflow/security/advisories/GHSA-vwmf-pq79-vjvx • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-33017-how-attackers-compromised-langflow-ai-pipelines-in-20-hours • https://www.sonicwall.com/blog/langflow-ai-code-injection-to-rce-flaw
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate end users running a genuinely shared Langflow playground flow via the public link
  • Langflow web UI itself issuing build_public_tmp calls during normal flow execution
  • Internal uptime/health-check monitors probing the API surface
  • Security scanners / vuln-management tools (Nessus, Qualys) fingerprinting the endpoint
  • Pen-test / red-team validation traffic from sanctioned source ranges
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request for each hit — check HTTP method (POST = build attempt), source IP reputation/geo, and whether the source is an external/internet IP vs the app's own UI host. 2) Contain: if external and unsanctioned, block the source IP at the WAF/proxy and confirm the Langflow instance version; if <= 1.9.1, take the public sharing offline and patch to >= 1.9.2. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2 on the Langflow host for python/uvicorn spawning shells in the same window, and review for credential/API-key access (.env, cloud metadata) given in-the-wild exploitation steals keys within hours.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/api/v1/build_public_tmp"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Requests=count(), Methods=make_set(HttpMethod), Statuses=make_set(HttpStatusCode), UAs=make_set(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent) by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, DstIpAddr, Url
| order by FirstSeen desc

Langflow backend (python/uvicorn) spawning OS shell or recon/exfil tool — RCE execution AIInstallation High
Detects the Langflow Python backend process (python/uvicorn/gunicorn running 'langflow') spawning a Unix shell, download utility, or recon binary — the post-exploitation signature of CVE-2026-48519, where injected custom-component Python passes through exec() and runs OS commands (PoC: 'touch /tmp/pwned'; in-the-wild: credential/API-key theft). Rationale: Built from the advisory's exec() RCE mechanism (custom Python in data.nodes[].data.node.template.code.value) and the PoC OS command 'touch /tmp/pwned' — a Langflow python/uvicorn parent spawning a shell or curl/wget/recon binary is high-fidelity because legitimate Langflow workers rarely shell out, and corroborating reports show in-the-wild exploitation steals keys via OS commands. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/langflow-ai/langflow/security/advisories/GHSA-vwmf-pq79-vjvx • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-33017-how-attackers-compromised-langflow-ai-pipelines-in-20-hours • https://cyberpress.org/langflow-ai-pipeline-rce-exploited/
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langflow custom components that legitimately shell out (e.g. a component invoking curl/git/subprocess by design)
  • Container entrypoint or startup scripts launching the langflow process via sh/bash wrappers
  • pip/uv/apt dependency installation spawned by the langflow runtime on first start
  • Admin debugging the running container with an interactive shell under the langflow process
  • Health-check or readiness probes that exec a shell inside the app container
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install","uv pip","apt-get","apt install","/usr/local/bin/docker-entrypoint"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: examine the child ProcessCommandLine — benign component shell-outs are predictable (known component logic); reverse shells, credential reads (.env, ~/.aws, cloud metadata 169.254.169.254), or base64/curl-to-attacker are malicious. Correlate with UC1 build_public_tmp hits on the same host/time. 2) Contain: isolate the Langflow host/container, kill the offending process tree, rotate any API keys/secrets reachable from the container, and patch to Langflow >= 1.9.2. 3) Hunt: review for dropped payloads, new cron/systemd persistence, outbound C2 from the langflow PID, and lateral movement using stolen credentials.

| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "langflow" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","curl","wget","nc","ncat","whoami","id","perl","ruby")
| where not(FileName in~ ("python","python3") and ProcessCommandLine has "langflow")

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vertex AI model upload to default predictable staging bucket (bucket-squat exposure) AIDelivery Medium
Surfaces Vertex AI ModelService.UploadModel operations that relied on the SDK's default deterministic staging bucket name ('{project}-vertex-staging-{region}') instead of an explicitly-pinned bucket. Per CVE-2026-2473, any upload using this default pattern is exposed to cross-tenant bucket squatting, so each hit must be checked to confirm the staging bucket is owned by your own project. Rationale: Anchored on the exact deterministic string '-vertex-staging-' from the article's gcs_utils.py snippet ('project + "-vertex-staging-" + location') plus the aiplatform UploadModel method; defender/sentinel/cloudwatch/falcon are empty because this telemetry only exists in GCP Cloud Audit Logs (no canonical Defender/Sentinel/AWS table). Cross-checked CVE and method behaviour against The Hacker News, CSO Online and GitLab advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/google-vertex-ai-sdk-flaw-let-attackers.html • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4186193/googles-vertex-ai-sdk-could-allow-rce-through-bucket-squatting.html • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pkg/pypi/google-cloud-aiplatform/CVE-2026-2473/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1525
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Routine ML pipeline uploads that intentionally use the default staging bucket already owned and pre-created in your own project
  • Data scientists running ad-hoc aiplatform.Model.upload() during model development
  • CI/CD model promotion jobs that never set staging_bucket explicitly
  • Notebook-driven experimentation where the same default bucket is reused across many uploads
Suppression filter
Refine in Datadog/Splunk by excluding uploads whose staging bucket is confirmed self-owned via a Reference Table of your project's known staging buckets, e.g. Splunk: | search NOT [ inputlookup owned_vertex_staging_buckets | fields bucket ]
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit, resolve the staging bucket name '{project}-vertex-staging-{region}' and run 'gsutil ls -L -b gs://<name>' / Storage API to confirm the bucket's owning project == your project. If owned elsewhere, you are squatted. 2) Contain: halt the deployment pipeline, delete/quarantine the uploaded model version, and pin an explicit attacker-proof staging_bucket; verify google-cloud-aiplatform is upgraded to >=1.148.0. 3) Hunt: enumerate all Vertex projects/regions for the same default pattern, check whether any squatted artifacts were already deployed (DeployModel), and review GCS object-access logs on the bucket for foreign principals.
title: Vertex AI Model Upload Using Default Predictable Staging Bucket
id: 7f3a1c2e-9b4d-4e6a-8c12-2a5b6d7e8f90
status: experimental
description: Detects Vertex AI model uploads that reference the SDK default deterministic staging bucket pattern '-vertex-staging-', exposed to cross-tenant bucket squatting (CVE-2026-2473).
references:

  keywords:

level: medium
source:gcp.audit @protoPayload.methodName:google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.ModelService.UploadModel vertex-staging
CLOUD
index=gcp sourcetype=google:gcp:pubsub:message "data.protoPayload.methodName"="google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.ModelService.UploadModel" "vertex-staging"
| rename data.protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail as principal, data.resource.labels.project_id as project, data.protoPayload.requestMetadata.callerIp as src_ip, data.protoPayload.resourceName as resource
| stats count min(_time) as firstSeen max(_time) as lastSeen values(resource) as resources by project, principal, src_ip

Foreign / non-Vertex principal accessing Vertex AI staging-bucket objects AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects GCS object create/delete/get operations on objects living in a '*-vertex-staging-*' bucket performed by a principal that is NOT the Vertex AI service agent (P4SA). This catches the attacker's model-replacement write (poisoning) and model-theft reads against a Vertex staging bucket you control, the core of the Pickle-in-the-Middle race window. Rationale: Targets the 'replace the legitimate model' tamper step and model theft by filtering storage.objects.* on the article's '-vertex-staging-' bucket pattern and excluding the legitimate Vertex P4SA (gcp-sa-aiplatform.iam.gserviceaccount.com); GCS data-access audit is GCP-only, hence empty Defender/Sentinel/AWS/Falcon fields. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/ • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4186193/googles-vertex-ai-sdk-could-allow-rce-through-bucket-squatting.html • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-2473/
ATT&CKT1530 T1565.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • The user or CI service account that performed the model upload writing artifacts into its own staging bucket
  • Backup or lifecycle tooling copying/cleaning objects in the staging bucket
  • A monitoring or DLP scanner doing storage.objects.get across all buckets
  • Terraform/infra automation managing staging bucket contents
Suppression filter
Add an allowlist of expected uploader identities, e.g. Datadog: append ' -@protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail:(your-ml-pipeline-sa@*.iam.gserviceaccount.com)'
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the principal and its source IP/project; determine whether it belongs to your org's IAM and whether it should ever touch staging buckets. Note object names — saved_model.pb, *.pkl, *.joblib being overwritten is high-signal. 2) Contain: revoke the principal's access to the bucket, lock the bucket (remove public/cross-project IAM), and block deployment of any model version staged during the access window. 3) Hunt: pull all DeployModel events that referenced affected artifacts, inspect deployed model artifacts for malicious pickle __reduce__ payloads, and rotate any credentials reachable from the Vertex serving environment.

| stats count min(_time) as firstSeen max(_time) as lastSeen values(method) as methods values(src_ip) as src_ips by principal, object
| sort - lastSeen
Vertex AI model deployment following default-staged upload (poisoned-model deploy) AIExploitation Medium
Correlates a Vertex AI ModelService.UploadModel that used the default '-vertex-staging-' bucket with a subsequent EndpointService.DeployModel in the same project within a short window. Deployment is the moment the staged (potentially attacker-replaced) artifact is loaded and the pickle/joblib payload executes in the serving container, so this is the last victim-visible checkpoint before RCE. Rationale: Pairs the default-staging UploadModel signal with the downstream DeployModel (the article's RCE trigger when joblib.load()/pickle.load() runs in the serving container); Sigma is empty because this is a temporal cross-event correlation, and the bare Datadog query surfaces deploys for rule-level correlation since Datadog cannot express the join inline. GCP-only telemetry, so non-GCP platform fields are empty. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/google-vertex-ai-sdk-flaw-let-attackers.html
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1525
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Normal MLOps flow where upload-then-deploy of a self-owned default-staged model is expected behaviour
  • Automated retraining pipelines that upload and immediately deploy on a schedule
  • Blue/green or canary endpoint rollouts deploying multiple model versions in quick succession
  • A/B experimentation deploying several models to the same endpoint within the window
Suppression filter
Scope the correlation to projects/SAs not on the approved MLOps allowlist, e.g. Splunk: append '| search NOT principal IN ("mlops-deployer@*.iam.gserviceaccount.com")'
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the upload's staging bucket is self-owned (see UC1); if ownership is uncertain or external, treat the deployed model as poisoned. 2) Contain: undeploy the model from the endpoint, delete the model version, and isolate/rotate any service-account credentials and secrets accessible from the Vertex serving environment (data exfil / lateral movement risk). 3) Hunt: inspect the deployed artifact for malicious pickle __reduce__ gadgets, review egress from the serving container's project, and sweep all projects for default-staged-then-deployed models on vulnerable SDK (<1.148.0).
source:gcp.audit @protoPayload.methodName:google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.EndpointService.DeployModel
CLOUD
index=gcp sourcetype=google:gcp:pubsub:message ("data.protoPayload.methodName"="google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.ModelService.UploadModel" OR "data.protoPayload.methodName"="google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.EndpointService.DeployModel")
| rename data.protoPayload.methodName as method, data.resource.labels.project_id as project, data.protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail as principal
| transaction project maxspan=60m startswith=eval(method="google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.ModelService.UploadModel") endswith=eval(method="google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.EndpointService.DeployModel")
| search "vertex-staging"
| table _time project principal method eventcount duration

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Dozens of malicious wallpapers found on Steam Workshop: gamers’ accounts at risk

Securelist (Kaspersky)
2026-06-16 15 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Since late 2025, malware has been spreading rapidly through the Steam Workshop, the gaming platform's built-in service for players to create and share custom content. The attackers are primarily targeting gamers in China and Russia.

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Steam wallpaper campaign payload hash sweep (DarkKomet / Lumma / Vidar / RenEngine)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Wallpaper Engine spawning LOLBins or staged binaries (Steam Workshop wallpaper malware) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Dozens of malicious wallpapers found on Steam Workshop: gamers’ accounts at risk
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Campaign loader '._cache_GAME1.exe' execution (Steam wallpaper malware) · [LLM] DarkKomet Synaptics.exe backdoor executing from ProgramData · [LLM] DarkKomet 'Synaptics Pointing Device Driver' Run-key persistence to ProgramData · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] C2 communication to Steam wallpaper campaign infrastructure (120.48.156.17 / 202.144.192.29) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Tampered AggregatorHost.dll loaded/dropped (Steam session credential theft) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Wallpaper Engine spawning LOLBins or staged binaries (Steam Workshop wallpaper malware) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts Wallpaper Engine host processes (wallpaper32.exe/wallpaper64.exe) spawning script interpreters, rundll32/regsvr32, the campaign loader/backdoor, or any child executing from Temp/AppData/ProgramData. Application-type wallpapers run arbitrary code, so a wallpaper process parenting a shell or an unsigned drop is the core execution signal of this campaign. Rationale: Anchors on Wallpaper Engine's documented host binaries as parent plus the campaign's named loader (._cache_), DarkKomet drop (Synaptics.exe), and user-writable execution paths. The parent+child pairing keeps it tighter than a bare LOLBin hunt. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/dozens-of-malicious-wallpapers-found-on-steam-workshop/120186/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/steam-workshop-abused-to-spread-malware-via-wallpaper-engine-app/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/steam-workshop-abused/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.001 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate application-type wallpaper (CPU/GPU widget, mini-game) that genuinely launches a helper exe from AppData
  • Wallpaper Engine auto-updater extracting and running an installer from %Temp%
  • Power-user wallpaper authors testing scenes that shell out to cmd/powershell
  • Steam overlay or anti-cheat helper spawned under the wallpaper process tree
Suppression filter
| where not(FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("-update","installer") and FolderPath has @"\Steam\steamapps\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child ProcessCommandLine and SHA256; check whether the parent wallpaper was installed via Steam Workshop in the last few days and whether the child is signed. 2) Contain: if the child is unsigned/from Temp or matches Synaptics.exe/._cache_, isolate the host and kill the process tree; quarantine the wallpaper package directory. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for AggregatorHost.dll loads, Synaptics.exe persistence, and outbound traffic to 120.48.156.17 / 202.144.192.29.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wallpaper32.exe","wallpaper64.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","Synaptics.exe")
    or FileName startswith "._cache_"
    or FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\ProgramData\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any (@"\wallpaper32.exe", @"\wallpaper64.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\cmd.exe", @"\powershell.exe", @"\pwsh.exe", @"\rundll32.exe", @"\regsvr32.exe", @"\mshta.exe", @"\wscript.exe", @"\cscript.exe", @"\Synaptics.exe", @"\._cache_", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\ProgramData\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 6f3c1d8a-2b41-4e9c-9a7d-7c2e1f0a4b55
description: Wallpaper Engine host process spawning a script interpreter, LOLBin, the campaign loader/backdoor, or a binary from a user-writable directory, consistent with malicious Steam Workshop application wallpapers.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/dozens-of-malicious-wallpapers-found-on-steam-workshop/120186/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/20
tags:

logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\wallpaper32.exe'
      - '\wallpaper64.exe'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\rundll32.exe'
      - '\regsvr32.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'

      - '\AppData\Local\Temp\'
      - '\AppData\Roaming\'
      - '\ProgramData\'
  condition: selection_parent and (selection_child or selection_path)
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\wallpaper32.exe OR *\\Wallpaper32.exe OR *\\wallpaper64.exe OR *\\Wallpaper64.exe) @Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\rundll32.exe OR *\\regsvr32.exe OR *\\mshta.exe OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\Synaptics.exe OR *\\._cache_* OR *\\Temp\\* OR *\\ProgramData\\*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/wallpaper(32|64)\.exe/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|rundll32|regsvr32|mshta|wscript|cscript|Synaptics|_cache_)/i OR ImageFileName=/\\(Temp|AppData|ProgramData)\\/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("wallpaper32.exe","wallpaper64.exe") AND (Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","Synaptics.exe") OR Processes.process IN ("*\\._cache_*.exe","*\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\*","*\\AppData\\Roaming\\*","*\\ProgramData\\*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

Campaign loader '._cache_GAME1.exe' execution (Steam wallpaper malware) AIInstallation High
Alerts on execution of the campaign's loader module whose filename begins with the distinctive '._cache_' prefix (e.g. ._cache_GAME1.exe). This module boots the decoy game NTRaholic while simultaneously sideloading the tampered AggregatorHost.dll Steam credential stealer. Rationale: The '._cache_GAME1.exe' string is a verbatim, highly distinctive code-block IOC from the article — the leading dot-underscore prefix is unusual enough on Windows that the prefix match alone is near-zero FP and double-confirmed by second-source write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/dozens-of-malicious-wallpapers-found-on-steam-workshop/120186/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/steam-workshop-abused/ • https://www.technadu.com/malicious-steam-workshop-wallpapers-hijack-accounts-via-wallpaper-engine-distribute-darkkomet-lumma-vidar-and-renengine/629591/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign application that legitimately uses a '._cache_'-prefixed temp executable naming convention (rare)
  • Security tooling re-detonating the sample in a sandbox on a monitored host
  • Backup/restore of a previously infected user profile re-surfacing the artifact
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the SHA256/MD5 and folder path of the ._cache_ process and its parent (expect a wallpaper package dir); confirm against the article hash set. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, and quarantine the parent wallpaper directory; block the hash org-wide. 3) Hunt: search the same host and others for AggregatorHost.dll image loads, Synaptics.exe drops in ProgramData, and C2 to 120.48.156.17/ey.php.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName startswith "._cache_"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has @"\._cache_"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DarkKomet Synaptics.exe backdoor executing from ProgramData AIInstallation High
Alerts when a process named Synaptics.exe runs from C:\ProgramData\Synaptics\ — the DarkKomet backdoor masquerading as the Synaptics touchpad driver, dropped by the malicious wallpaper. The legitimate Synaptics driver runs from Program Files / DriverStore, never from ProgramData\Synaptics, making the path a clean discriminator. Rationale: Second sources (Trend Micro DarkKomet encyclopedia, CyberSecurityNews) confirm the backdoor drops to C:\ProgramData\Synaptics\Synaptics.exe under the 'Synaptics Pointing Device Driver' guise; the ProgramData\Synaptics path is the discriminator that separates malware from the genuine driver. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/dozens-of-malicious-wallpapers-found-on-steam-workshop/120186/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/steam-workshop-abused/ • https://www.trendmicro.com/vinfo/us/threat-encyclopedia/malware/backdoor.msil.darkkomet.ac
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A rare OEM/driver utility that stages a Synaptics helper under ProgramData (verify signature)
  • Endpoint backup/imaging tooling restoring a previously infected profile
  • Security sandbox detonating the sample on a monitored host
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the binary's signature (DarkKomet is unsigned or fake-signed) and hash against the campaign IOC set; check the parent process for a wallpaper/loader origin. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill Synaptics.exe, and delete the C:\ProgramData\Synaptics directory and its Run-key persistence value. 3) Hunt: look for the 'Synaptics Pointing Device Driver' Run value pointing to ProgramData, AggregatorHost.dll loads, and DarkKomet C2 beacons.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "Synaptics.exe"
| where FolderPath has @"\ProgramData\Synaptics\"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\Synaptics.exe"
| where NewProcessName has @"\ProgramData\Synaptics\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Tampered AggregatorHost.dll loaded/dropped (Steam session credential theft) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts for the malicious AggregatorHost.dll — a tampered system-library name sideloaded by ._cache_GAME1.exe to locate the Steam client and hijack the live session. Windows ships AggregatorHost.exe, not a DLL by this name, so any AggregatorHost.dll outside System32/SysWOW64 is anomalous. Rationale: AggregatorHost.dll is named verbatim in the article and confirmed by second sources as the patched library that hunts the Steam client and hijacks the session; keying on the DLL name plus a System32/SysWOW64 exclusion makes any hit high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/dozens-of-malicious-wallpapers-found-on-steam-workshop/120186/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/steam-workshop-abused-to-spread-malware-via-wallpaper-engine-app/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/steam-workshop-abused/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1539 T1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Security product detonating the sample on an instrumented host
  • Telemetry from a malware-analysis VM in the monitored estate
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the loading process (expect ._cache_GAME1.exe or a wallpaper binary) and hash the DLL; confirm the host has the Steam client and an active session. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate the loader, quarantine the DLL, and force a Steam credential/session reset for the user (revoke active sessions, change password). 3) Hunt: pivot to outbound traffic to 120.48.156.17/ey.php, Synaptics.exe persistence, and any other hosts loading AggregatorHost.dll from non-system paths.

| where FileName =~ "AggregatorHost.dll"
| where not(FolderPath has @"\Windows\System32\" or FolderPath has @"\Windows\SysWOW64\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, MD5, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, TargetFileMD5
| order by TimeGenerated desc

C2 communication to Steam wallpaper campaign infrastructure (120.48.156.17 / 202.144.192.29) AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any host connecting to the campaign's confirmed C2 IPs or the specific exfil/download URLs (ey.php, audit.php, download2/Themes2.zip). AggregatorHost.dll posts stolen Steam session data to 120.48.156.17/ey.php; 202.144.192.29 serves second-stage payloads. Rationale: 120.48.156.17/ey.php is a verbatim code-block IOC and 202.144.192.29 (with audit.php and download2/Themes2.zip) is in the article's IOC list; both confirmed across second-source write-ups. Hardcoded IP/URL matches are inherently low-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/dozens-of-malicious-wallpapers-found-on-steam-workshop/120186/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/steam-workshop-abused/ • https://www.technadu.com/malicious-steam-workshop-wallpapers-hijack-accounts-via-wallpaper-engine-distribute-darkkomet-lumma-vidar-and-renengine/629591/

Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process (expect AggregatorHost.dll host, Synaptics.exe, or a wallpaper binary) and the bytes/direction of the flow to gauge exfil vs download. 2) Contain: block both IPs at the perimeter, isolate the host, and reset/revoke the user's Steam session and password. 3) Hunt: sweep all hosts for these IPs over 90 days, then pivot on each hit to AggregatorHost.dll loads and Synaptics.exe persistence.

DarkKomet 'Synaptics Pointing Device Driver' Run-key persistence to ProgramData AIInstallation High
Alerts when a CurrentVersion\Run value (commonly named 'Synaptics Pointing Device Driver') is set with data pointing to C:\ProgramData\Synaptics\Synaptics.exe. The malware reuses the genuine driver's value name but redirects it to ProgramData, so the value DATA path is the discriminator from the legitimate Program Files entry. Rationale: Second sources document the exact persistence: a Run value 'Synaptics Pointing Device Driver' redirected to C:\ProgramData\Synaptics\Synaptics.exe. Matching the value DATA path (ProgramData\Synaptics) avoids FPs from the legitimate driver, which targets Program Files. Datadog left empty: the provided Sysmon schema exposes @TargetObject (the key/value name) but not the value DATA, and the value name alone matches the genuine driver — so a clean Datadog expression isn't possible on this tenant's fields. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/dozens-of-malicious-wallpapers-found-on-steam-workshop/120186/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/steam-workshop-abused/ • https://www.trendmicro.com/vinfo/us/threat-encyclopedia/malware/backdoor.msil.darkkomet.ac
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An OEM utility that genuinely stages a Synaptics helper under ProgramData and registers autorun (verify signature — extremely rare)
  • Profile/image restore re-applying a previously planted Run value
  • Security sandbox detonation on a monitored host
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the Run value DATA resolves to ProgramData\Synaptics\Synaptics.exe and the target binary is unsigned/matches campaign hashes; note the writing process. 2) Contain: isolate the host, delete the Run value and the ProgramData\Synaptics directory, and terminate any running Synaptics.exe. 3) Hunt: enumerate other hosts for the same Run-value data, AggregatorHost.dll loads, and C2 to 120.48.156.17.

| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueData has @"\ProgramData\Synaptics\Synaptics.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent

| where RegistryValueData has @"\ProgramData\Synaptics\Synaptics.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Steam wallpaper campaign payload hash sweep (DarkKomet / Lumma / Vidar / RenEngine) AIDelivery Medium
Retrospective and forward IOC sweep for the 13 MD5 hashes published for this campaign across process executions and file writes. Catches any campaign payload variant (DarkKomet backdoor, Lumma/Vidar stealers, RenEngine downloader, miners) regardless of filename or delivery packaging. Rationale: Uses the 13 published MD5 IOCs verbatim across both process and file telemetry so it catches any payload family in the campaign irrespective of filename/packaging. Datadog uses uppercase hex because Sysmon emits @Hashes in uppercase; KQL/Splunk/Falcon use the article's lowercase with case-insensitive matching. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/dozens-of-malicious-wallpapers-found-on-steam-workshop/120186/ • https://www.technadu.com/malicious-steam-workshop-wallpapers-hijack-accounts-via-wallpaper-engine-distribute-darkkomet-lumma-vidar-and-renengine/629591/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1588.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security analyst or sandbox detonating a sample on a monitored host
  • AV/EDR quarantine copy re-hashed in a watched directory
  • Malware-research VM telemetry inside the monitored estate
  • Hash collision (negligible for MD5 at this scale but theoretically possible)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the matched hash and the host/user; determine whether the file executed or was only written, and identify the parent (wallpaper/loader). 2) Contain: isolate the host, block all 13 hashes org-wide, and reset the affected user's Steam credentials/sessions. 3) Hunt: from each hit pivot to AggregatorHost.dll loads, Synaptics.exe persistence, and C2 to 120.48.156.17 / 202.144.192.29; review Steam Workshop download history on the host.

C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
