            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Tracing Digital Intent: New MacOS Tahoe 26 Artifact Discovered
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Budibase global-admin escalation via POST /api/public/v1/roles/assign (CVE-2026-48150) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP POSTs to Budibase's public-API roles/assign endpoint, the exact sink CVE-2026-48150 abuses to grant builder.global/admin.global to arbitrary user IDs. This endpoint is a niche Enterprise (EXPANDED_PUBLIC_API) surface; any POST to it on an unpatched (<3.39.0) tenant is worth a builder-role review since the HTTP layer cannot distinguish a legitimate global admin from an escalating workspace-scoped builder. Rationale: Uses the literal vulnerable endpoint path '/api/public/v1/roles/assign' + POST method from the advisory PoC; this public-API route is rarely called in normal operation, making method+path a high-signal pivot for the CVE-2026-48150 mass-assignment sink. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6xp4-cf37-ppjh • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@budibase/server/CVE-2026-48150/ • https://docs.budibase.com/reference/roleassign • https://www.thehackerwire.com/budibase-critical-privilege-escalation-cve-2026-48150/
ATT&CKT1068 T1098
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate global admin using the public API / integration to assign or revoke roles in bulk
  • Automation or IaC pipeline that provisions Budibase users via the public API and calls roles/assign
  • Penetration-test or vulnerability-scanner traffic replaying the CVE PoC against the tenant
  • SCIM/SSO provisioning middleware that wraps the public roles endpoint
  • Internal QA/staging environment role seeding scripts
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("10.0.0.5")  // exclude known SSO/IaC provisioning host once identified during baselining
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: From the source IP/host, pull the Budibase identity behind the API key used (x-budibase-api-key) and confirm whether that caller already holds builder.global or admin.global. A caller who is only a workspace-scoped builder (builder.apps set, builder.global unset) = confirmed exploit. 2) CONTAIN: Revoke the offending API key (regenerate via global self/api_key admin), reset the affected users' roles, and verify no user unexpectedly gained admin.global; upgrade the instance to Budibase 3.39.0+. 3) HUNT: Enumerate all userIds granted builder/admin global since the first POST, check for follow-on access to datasource credentials, SCIM/OIDC/audit-log config changes, and automation exports performed under the newly elevated identities.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| where Url has "/api/public/v1/roles/assign"
| summarize Requests = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Statuses = make_set(HttpStatusCode), UserAgents = make_set(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent) by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, HttpMethod
| order by LastSeen desc
WEB

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.status) as status values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agent from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=POST Web.url="*/api/public/v1/roles/assign*" by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.http_method

Budibase self-minted API key followed by global-role assignment (CVE-2026-48150 chain) AIExploitation Medium
Correlates a GET /api/global/self/api_key (the attacker minting an API key tied to their own identity) with a POST /api/public/v1/roles/assign from the same source within a short window — the exact two-step flow in the CVE-2026-48150 PoC where Alice mints a key then escalates herself/another user to global admin. Pairing the key-mint with the escalation removes most legitimate single-action noise. Rationale: Chains the two literal PoC paths ('/api/global/self/api_key' GET to mint, '/api/public/v1/roles/assign' POST to escalate) on the same source within 1h, matching the advisory's Step 2 to Step 3 attack flow; the temporal pairing is far higher fidelity than either request alone. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6xp4-cf37-ppjh • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@budibase/server/CVE-2026-48150/ • https://docs.budibase.com/reference/roleassign
ATT&CKT1098 T1068
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An administrator legitimately generating a personal API key then using the public API to manage roles in one session
  • Onboarding automation that mints a service API key and immediately seeds user roles
  • Developer testing the public API end-to-end against a non-prod tenant
  • Shared egress NAT collapsing two different users (one minting a key, another assigning roles) to the same SrcIpAddr
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the Budibase user who minted the API key (GET self/api_key returns the userId) and check their pre-existing scope — a workspace-scoped builder minting a key then POSTing roles/assign is the confirmed CVE-2026-48150 chain. 2) CONTAIN: Revoke that API key, restore the affected users' original roles (note the SDK overwrites builder.apps scope, so re-apply scoping), and patch to 3.39.0+. 3) HUNT: Review all role grants from that identity, look for the follow-up 'admin:true' self-grant POST, and audit datasource/automation/SCIM access performed after the grant timestamp.
let window = 1h;
let keymint = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where Url has "/api/global/self/api_key"
    | project KeyMintTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| where Url has "/api/public/v1/roles/assign"
| join kind=inner keymint on SrcIpAddr
| where TimeGenerated between (KeyMintTime .. KeyMintTime + window)  // key minted then used to escalate within 1h
| project KeyMintTime, AssignTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, HttpStatusCode
| order by AssignTime desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where match(urls,"api_key") AND match(urls,"roles/assign")
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime

Package-manager supply-chain control bypass via pnpm minimumReleaseAge=0 AIInstallation High
Hunts for npm/pnpm/yarn install invocations that explicitly set minimumReleaseAge=0 on the command line, disabling pnpm 11's default new-package quarantine window. This is the exact bypass the article cites (an AI coding agent running `pnpm install --config.minimumReleaseAge=0`), which re-opens the exposure window during which freshly published malicious packages are most dangerous. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim code block `pnpm install --config.minimumReleaseAge=0`; the value `=0` is the high-fidelity discriminator (legitimate hardening sets a positive minute count like 1440/10080, never 0). Cross-checked against pnpm's own supply-chain docs and a pnpm 11 write-up confirming 1440-minute default and that 0 disables the control. Cross-checked against: • https://pnpm.io/supply-chain-security • https://cybersecuritynews.com/pnpm-11-turns-on-minimum-release-age/ • https://pnpm.io/settings
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CI/CD build agent deliberately running with minimumReleaseAge=0 to always resolve latest dependencies
  • Developer pulling a legitimate security hotfix published inside the quarantine window
  • AI coding agent self-unblocking on a needed dependency (the article's own sanctioned-but-risky scenario)
  • Container image build step that bootstraps a monorepo and disables the delay for speed
  • Internal package-publish smoke tests that install their own just-published artifact
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full command line, parent process, and user/host. Determine if it ran under an interactive developer session or a CI/build agent, and whether the install pulled any package published within the last 24h. 2) Contain: if non-sanctioned, kill the install, quarantine the host's node_modules/lockfile delta, and block the resolved package versions pending review; require minimumReleaseAge to remain at the org default. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/user for newly installed packages (FileWritten under node_modules), outbound connections from node.exe to non-registry domains, and any postinstall script execution (node/npm spawning cmd/powershell) in the minutes after install.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "minimumReleaseAge"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)minimumReleaseAge\s*=\s*0(\D|$)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "minimumReleaseAge"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)minimumReleaseAge\s*=\s*0(\D|$)"
| where not(Account endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-35273")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-35273")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)

| order by files desc

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35") or SHA1 in~ ("f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35") or MD5 in~ ("f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35") or SHA1 in~ ("f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35") or MD5 in~ ("f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

A tale of two eras

Cisco Talos
2026-06-11 7 use cases 1 technique 5 kill-chain phases detected

In this week’s newsletter, Amy reminisces on the tech toys of their childhood, inspired by a hilarious lesson about why your digital privacy shouldn't be left on an open channel.

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — A tale of two eras
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Talos most-prevalent CoinMiner / W32.Injector / Win.Dropper.Miner file-hash watchlist · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Talos most-prevalent CoinMiner / W32.Injector / Win.Dropper.Miner file-hash watchlist AIInstallation Medium
Hunts execution or on-disk drop of the four specific malware binaries Talos flagged as most-prevalent this week (Win.Worm.Coinminer 'VID001.exe', W32.Injector:Gen.21ie, Win.Dropper.Miner) by exact SHA256/MD5. Article-specific because it pins the named hashes from the Talos telemetry block rather than a generic miner/injector behaviour. Rationale: Pins the exact SHA256/MD5 pairs Talos published as most-prevalent (CoinMiner 'VID001.exe' 9f1f..., W32.Injector 96fa..., Win.Dropper.Miner a31f..., dropper 9896...). Hash-exact match is the only article-specific high-fidelity signal available; the article carries no command-lines or process trees. Cross-checked against Hybrid Analysis sandbox report and CIS Top 10 Malware before shipping. Cross-checked against: • https://hybrid-analysis.com/sample/9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507 • https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/top-10-malware-q4-2025 • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/a-tale-of-two-eras/
ATT&CKT1496 T1055.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis / detonation VM where a researcher intentionally ran the sample (sandbox host)
  • EDR or AV quarantine copy of the file being written to a vault path, re-firing the file-write branch
  • Threat-intel ingestion tooling that stages known-bad samples to disk for YARA/hash enrichment
  • IR collection host where the sample was copied off a victim for examination
  • Vulnerable-by-design / red-team lab images that purposely host prevalent malware corpora
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("SANDBOX01","MALWARE-ANALYSIS","IR-VAULT") and FolderPath !has @"\Quarantine\" and FolderPath !has @"\AV_Quarantine\"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the DeviceName/aid is a production endpoint, not a sandbox or IR analysis host; pull the FolderPath, initiating process and signing status, and check whether it was ProcessCreated (executed) vs only dropped. Step 2 (contain): If executed on a production host, network-isolate the device via Defender/Falcon, kill and quarantine the binary, and capture the parent process for the delivery vector. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the same SHA256/MD5 org-wide, then check for CoinMiner follow-on — high sustained CPU, outbound stratum/mining-pool connections, and WMI Event Consumer persistence — and for injector activity look for the dropped child under the same logon session.

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98") or SHA1 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98") or MD5 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98") or SHA1 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98") or MD5 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CodeIgniter4 ext_in bypass: PHP-extension file written into web-accessible upload dir AIInstallation High
Hunts the artifact of CVE-2026-48062: a file with a PHP-executable extension (shell.php, .phtml, .phar) written by a PHP runtime or web-server process into an uploads/avatar/writable directory. The ext_in bypass lets GIF-content-but-.php-named files survive validation and land via $file->move($path) under the web root. Rationale: Anchored on the CVE-2026-48062 bypass artifact: $file->move($path) preserving a client-supplied PHP extension (shell.php) in CodeIgniter's web-accessible upload paths (uploads/avatar/writable named in the advisory workarounds), written specifically by a PHP/web-server process. Cross-checked GitLab advisory and CodeIgniter GitHub security advisories (fix v4.7.3, CWE-434). Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/codeigniter4/framework/CVE-2026-48062/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2gr4-ppc7-7mhx • https://github.com/codeigniter4/CodeIgniter4/security/advisories
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CodeIgniter/Composer writing compiled PHP view/cache files (.php) under writable/cache during legitimate operation
  • Admin-initiated CMS/plugin/theme upload that legitimately deploys .php templates into the web root
  • Application self-update or artisan/spark commands generating PHP files under public/
  • Backup or staging tooling copying a full PHP app tree into wwwroot/htdocs
  • Developer deploying code via a web-based file manager
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has "writable\\cache" or FileName startswith "ci_session") and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("composer","spark","artisan"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the dropped file (FolderPath/SHA256) — confirm it is a single user-uploaded .php in an uploads/avatar dir (not framework cache); inspect contents for GIF magic header + PHP tags (<?php, eval, system, base64_decode) confirming the polyglot bypass. 2) Contain: quarantine/remove the file, revoke web-server execute permission on the upload directory, and block the uploading source IP at the WAF; isolate the host if the file already executed. 3) Hunt: pull the web logs for GET/POST to that exact path (UC2), check for php/php-cgi spawning shells (UC3), and verify the CodeIgniter4 version — anything <4.7.3 is vulnerable; review the app's upload validation chain for reliance on ext_in.

| where FolderPath has_any ("uploads","avatar","writable","wwwroot","htdocs","public","www")

| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

Webshell access: HTTP request to a .php file under a CodeIgniter upload/avatar path AICommand & Control Medium
Detects HTTP requests that successfully retrieve/execute a PHP file living under an uploads, avatar or writable directory — i.e. invocation of a webshell planted via the CVE-2026-48062 ext_in bypass. Legitimate CodeIgniter routes funnel through index.php, so a directly-served .php under an upload path is highly abnormal. Rationale: Uses the advisory's specific upload directories (uploads/writable) plus the avatar field from the documented vulnerable rule string; in a CodeIgniter4 app all routing goes through index.php, so a 200 on a .php served directly from an upload path is a strong webshell-invocation signal. Defender/Falcon/Datadog left empty: inbound HTTP URI telemetry is not present in EDR/FDR — this detection lives in web-server logs only. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/codeigniter4/framework/CVE-2026-48062/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2gr4-ppc7-7mhx
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legacy/non-CodeIgniter app on the same host that legitimately serves .php from a gallery or /images/ path (e.g. a thumbnailer script)
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Acunetix) probing upload paths for .php and receiving 200 from a benign placeholder
  • Rewrite rules that map /uploads/<x>.php through to index.php returning 200 for a non-existent file
  • Legitimate file-manager plugin that stores and serves editable .php snippets
  • Monitoring/uptime checks hitting a known .php health endpoint under a public path
Suppression filter
| where not (csUserAgent has_any ("Nessus","Acunetix","nmap","masscan","Nuclei")) and csUriStem !endswith "/index.php"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the exact csUriStem and check whether that .php file exists on disk under the upload dir (correlate with UC1) and whether it was recently created; review csUserAgent and cIP for scanner vs interactive-shell patterns and look at csUriQuery for command params (cmd=, c=, exec=). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, remove the file, and disable execution in the upload directory (deny handler / php_admin_flag engine off). 3) Hunt: enumerate every distinct .php under upload paths accessed in the window, pivot to host process telemetry (UC3) for php/php-cgi spawning shells, and review all source IPs that touched the same file for lateral access.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem endswith ".php" or csUriStem endswith ".phtml" or csUriStem endswith ".phar" or csUriStem endswith ".pht"
| where csUriStem has_any ("/uploads/","/avatar","/writable/","/images/")
| where scStatus == 200
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent, csUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PHP runtime or web server spawning a shell/LOLBin (CodeIgniter webshell RCE) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects a PHP interpreter or web-server process (php-cgi, php-fpm, httpd, nginx) spawning a command shell or recon/download LOLBin — the post-exploitation execution that follows a webshell dropped via the CVE-2026-48062 ext_in bypass. PHP runtimes legitimately almost never spawn cmd/powershell/bash/whoami. Rationale: Targets the RCE consequence of the bypass: a webshell's PHP code calling system()/exec(), which manifests as php-cgi/php-fpm/httpd as parent of cmd/powershell/sh/whoami. Parent set is restricted to PHP/web runtimes (w3wp deliberately excluded) so the parent->child pair is inherently high-fidelity for the CodeIgniter RCE chain described in the advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/codeigniter4/framework/CVE-2026-48062/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2gr4-ppc7-7mhx
ATT&CKT1059 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • PHP app legitimately shelling out to ImageMagick/ffmpeg via system() for avatar/thumbnail processing (often invokes sh -c)
  • Composer/Laravel/CI scheduled jobs (spark/cron) spawning git, curl or php subprocesses for deploy or webhook delivery
  • PHP-based monitoring/health scripts running whoami or net to report context
  • CI/CD agent running under php-fpm invoking build tooling
  • Legitimate admin plugin offering a 'system info' page that calls uname/whoami
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("convert","ffmpeg","imagemagick","gs ","/usr/bin/git") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("spark","artisan","composer"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full ProcessCommandLine of the child and the InitiatingProcessCommandLine of the PHP parent; benign image-processing calls reference convert/ffmpeg with file paths, whereas whoami/net/curl-to-external or interactive cmd are malicious — confirm the PHP working directory is an upload path. 2) Contain: kill the process tree, isolate the host, and pull execute permissions on the upload directory; preserve the parent PHP script for forensics. 3) Hunt: correlate back to the dropped file (UC1) and webshell access logs (UC2), search for follow-on persistence/credential access from the same host, and confirm CodeIgniter4 is patched to >=4.7.3.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php.exe","php-cgi.exe","php-fpm","httpd.exe","apache2","nginx")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh","bash","dash","whoami.exe","whoami","net.exe","net1.exe","curl.exe","curl","wget","certutil.exe","python.exe","python3")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php","php-cgi","php-fpm","httpd","apache","nginx")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell","pwsh","/bin/sh","bash","dash","whoami","net.exe","curl","wget","certutil","python")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
